Revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman suspected of being a Chinese spy have forced the chipmaker's board to confront more than ordinary executive misconduct, raising ​existential questions for the company and concerns about the board's ability to investigate its CEO independently.

Among corporate leaders, "There have definitely been ‌affair scandals and sexual-harassment scandals. But honey-pot scandals? No," said Ann Lipton, a University of Colorado law professor who follows boardroom issues.

She was using a term for an espionage ploy in which an operative entraps a target by feigning romantic interest. Historical examples include the Profumo Affair in the early 1960s and tend to involve diplomatic or political consequences.

US President Donald Trump ​said on Monday the FBI was probing Huang's relationship, a day after Nvidia's board launched an internal investigation "regarding the national security concerns raised in news ​reports, ," according to an email Huang sent to Nvidia employees and released by the company.

The company's advanced semiconductors are at the ⁠heart of a global race for AI superiority. China's Foreign Ministry said the spying claim was "a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear."

Nvidia co-founder Huang, 63, has ​no obvious successor and close ties to Trump. He owns 3.6% of its stock and has dozens of direct reports, suggesting a tight grip on the company.

Shares ​in Nvidia fell Monday as Huang's future came under scrutiny. But the stock later trimmed its decline to close 4% lower as some investors bet that the CEO could survive the crisis.

Board's credibility

Unusually among its peers, Nvidia operates without a board chair among its 11 directors. While the company considers all but Huang independent, three independent directors have served since the 1990s ​and a fourth, Mark Stevens, for most of that time. Only two have joined the board since 2021.

The clubby roster may not be so unusual ​by the standards of charismatic Silicon Valley company founders like Apple's Steve Jobs, who died in 2011.

But the US probe has heightened scrutiny of whether directors who have worked alongside ‌Huang for ⁠decades are sufficiently independent to investigate his conduct.

"If you have a figure like Steve Jobs, I think people on Wall Street as well as in Silicon Valley would say they're entitled to some leeway or deference," said Marc Goldstein, head of US research for proxy adviser Institutional Shareholder Services.

Such deference could now raise questions about whether the board provided sufficient oversight of a CEO whose own judgment has come under scrutiny.

Nvidia said on Sunday that while its board had no ​reason to believe that either US national ​security or Nvidia secrets were ⁠compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information. The board said it had confidence in the CEO and his leadership team.

Goldstein said board members running that investigation should be given the latitude to hire their own legal advisers to bolster their ​credibility.

The company also might consider keeping long-serving directors away from the probe, he added, to avoid legal challenges from ​shareholders claiming it wasn't ⁠sufficiently independent.

Yale University management professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld said the company faces additional national-security questions because of the ties between Huang and Trump. Trump, who has praised Huang, said on Monday that he had spoken to the executive and thought he would "be in good shape."

Washington has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China since 2022. Last ⁠year the ​Trump administration allowed Nvidia to resume certain China shipments under arrangements in which the US ​government receives a cut of the company's China chip sales.

The deal makes any suggestion of foreign espionage more sensitive for both executives and US government officials, Sonnenfeld said. "That's why you don't want state ​capitalism arrangements. You don't want the US government to be so involved in private companies," he said.

headline: Imam-ul-Haq, Abdullah Shafique hit centuries in Quaid-e-Azam Trophy Gold
description: Rawalpindi, Abbottabad seal innings victories in Silver competition of the first-class event
author: Sports Desk
article_text:
Centuries by Imam-ul-Haq, Abdullah Shafique and Azeem Bari headlined the second day of the second round of the Quaid-e-Azam Trophy Gold with Islamabad also building a commanding position against Lahore Whites on Tuesday.

At the Diamond Cricket Ground in Islamabad, Imam struck an unbeaten 137 to help Multan reach 216 in reply to Karachi Blues' 214. Asad Umar claimed 6-45 to put Multan in a strong position. Karachi Blues were 72-1 in their second innings at stumps, holding a lead of 70 runs.

Abdullah Shafique scored 112 as Sialkot Blues reached 316-9 in reply to Faisalabad's 222 at Shoaib Akhtar Cricket Stadium in Rawalpindi. Abdul Rehman supported him with 53, while Asad Raza took three wickets for Faisalabad.

At the Abbottabad Cricket Stadium, Islamabad piled up 403-6 against Lahore Whites after resuming at 113-1. Azeem Bari led the scoring with 105 while Raja Hamza Waheed made 74, Sudais Ulfat scored 67 and Sarmad Bhatti remained unbeaten on 70. Noman Ali took four wickets for 112 runs.

At National Ground in Islamabad, FATA were dismissed for 230 in reply to Peshawar Blues' 220. Salman Khan Jnr scored 71, while Niaz Khan claimed four wickets. Peshawar reached 150-4 in their second innings, establishing a lead of 140 runs. Shaheen Shah Afridi took three wickets for 36.

Quaid-e-Azam Trophy Silver

Rawalpindi and Abbottabad registered emphatic innings victories on the second day of the Silver competition.

Rawalpindi defeated Larkana by an innings and 239 runs at KCCA Stadium in Karachi. After posting 437 in their first innings, Rawalpindi bowled out Larkana for 57 and 141. Mohammad Nabeel claimed four wickets for 30 in the second innings, while Mohammad Nawaz took five in the first.

Abbottabad secured an even bigger victory, beating DMJ by an innings and 304 runs at Multan Cricket Stadium. Mohammad Riazullah remained unbeaten on 178 as Abbottabad posted 402. Israr Hussain took four wickets in each innings, helping dismiss DMJ for 30 and 68.

Elsewhere, Hyderabad were 200-2 against AJK, with Sardar Hassan Raza Khan unbeaten on 107, while Sialkot Whites reached 35 without loss in their second innings against Karachi Whites.

headline: Elon Musk voices support for Russell Brand after sexual assault conviction
description: Megyn Kelly also challenged the jury’s decision, while other conservative figures have remained silent
author: Pop Culture, Art
article_text:
Elon Musk has weighed in on Russell Brand’s criminal conviction, questioning the legal standard behind the case after the former comedian was found guilty of rape and sexual assault in the UK.

The tech billionaire responded to a post on X mocking Brand’s conviction, describing the legal standard as “crazy”. His remarks came a day after conservative commentator Megyn Kelly publicly challenged the jury’s decision, expressing disbelief at the outcome.

Kelly said she did not accept the charges simply because the jury had reached a guilty verdict. She also described Brand as a conservative figure who had been targeted.

Brand was sentenced on Monday to 10 and a half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The allegations included an incident in which a woman said Brand had sex with her without consent, leaving her bleeding and in pain. Brand maintained that the encounter was consensual.

Musk’s intervention has drawn attention to the support Brand has received from prominent American commentators, particularly those associated with anti-establishment politics. Brand has built a substantial online following through videos discussing government authority, the media, Covid-19 vaccination campaigns and other political issues.

His political positioning has changed over the years. Brand was once associated with left-wing activism and called for socialist policies during a 2013 appearance on BBC’s Newsnight. His online commentary became increasingly conservative and conspiratorial during the coronavirus pandemic, helping him attract an American audience.

Tucker Carlson, who previously interviewed Brand and expressed concern about the possibility of a prison sentence, has not publicly commented on the conviction. Donald Trump Jr. had also appeared on Brand’s programme in 2024.

Musk’s response adds another prominent name to the public debate surrounding Brand’s case, although his criticism does not change the jury’s verdict or the sentence imposed by the court.

Brand was sentenced on Monday to 10 and a half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The allegations included an incident in which a woman said Brand had sex with her without consent, leaving her bleeding and in pain. Brand maintained that the encounter was consensual.

Musk’s intervention has drawn attention to the support Brand has received from prominent American commentators, particularly those associated with anti-establishment politics. Brand has built a substantial online following through videos discussing government authority, the media, Covid-19 vaccination campaigns and other political issues.

His political positioning has changed over the years. Brand was once associated with left-wing activism and called for socialist policies during a 2013 appearance on BBC’s Newsnight. His online commentary became increasingly conservative and conspiratorial during the coronavirus pandemic, helping him attract an American audience.

Tucker Carlson, who previously interviewed Brand and expressed concern about the possibility of a prison sentence, has not publicly commented on the conviction. Donald Trump Jr. had also appeared on Brand’s programme in 2024.

Musk’s response adds another prominent name to the public debate surrounding Brand’s case, although his criticism does not change the jury’s verdict or the sentence imposed by the court.

headline: Pakistan, US seek closer academic and think tank exchanges
description: Pakistan, US seek closer academic and think tank exchanges
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Pakistan and the United States on Tuesday agreed to promote closer exchanges between think tanks and academic institutions to deepen mutual understanding and encourage dialogue on regional and international issues.

The understanding was reached during a meeting between Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Senator Ishaq Dar and former US assistant secretary of state for South Asian affairs Ambassador Robin Raphel, according to a statement issued by the Foreign Office.

The statement said the two sides discussed matters of mutual interest.

Dar appreciated the positive trajectory of Pakistan-US relations and underscored the importance of sustained engagement to further strengthen bilateral cooperation.

Both sides agreed to encourage closer exchanges between think tanks and academic institutions in the two countries to promote mutual understanding and dialogue on regional and international issues.

Earlier today, US President Donald Trump nominated Chargé d’Affaires Natalie A Baker as the next US ambassador to Pakistan, paving the way for the appointment of a permanent envoy to Islamabad after a gap of nearly two years.

The White House announced the nomination in a list of appointments sent to the US Senate on Monday.

Her nomination is subject to confirmation by the US Senate. If confirmed, Natalie will become the first US ambassador to Pakistan since Donald Blome left the post in early 2025.

The Pakistan-US relationship experienced a significant thaw in 2025–2026, transitioning from a cold period to warm, strategic, and pragmatic engagement during Trump's second term. This shift was largely driven by a major reset in relations following President Trump's intervention in regional conflicts, particularly his role in brokering a ceasefire between Pakistan and India in May 2025.

The first thaw in Pakistan-US relations came via secret counterterrorism exchanges, signalling substantive cooperation. In March last year, Trump unexpectedly praised Pakistan’s counterterrorism efforts during a national address, prompting a policy shift.

The short but intense May skirmish with India in May 2025 became a decisive turning point, showcasing Pakistan’s military discipline, strategic focus, and asymmetric capabilities — qualities that reportedly surprised Trump.

Despite India’s repeated denials, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif continued to praise President Trump for his role in brokering a ceasefire between the two nuclear-armed neighbours, and nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize, saying his intervention had helped save millions of lives.

The praise was reciprocated, with Trump commending the premier and also lauding CDF Munir, as he reiterated claims that he had helped avert a war between Pakistan and India in May 2025.

Ties between the countries took a further turn when Trump invited CDF Munir to a luncheon — the first such meeting for a Pakistani military chief — followed by a red-carpet visit to US Central Command headquarters for high-level talks.

Following a ceasefire after the prolonged war in Gaza, Trump announced the formation of a “Board of Peace” that included Pakistan, again singling out PM Shehbaz for praise during its inaugural summit.

Addressing the event, Trump said, “I like this guy,” referring to the premier, as he recounted efforts that led to last year’s ceasefire between Pakistan and India. He also praised CDF Munir during his remarks.

In June this year, President Trump credited Pakistan with “really helping” the United States secure a peace deal with Iran while especially praising Chief of Defence Forces Field Marshal Asim Munir and PM Shehbaz.

“In Pakistan, you have Field Marshal Asim Munir, who is great, and you have the Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and they just get along great,” he said during an interview with Axios.

headline: Punjab plans central authority to take control of public assets
description: Proposed law faces criticism over bureaucracy, weaker local powers and reduced public accountability.
author: Muhammad Ilyas
article_text:
Who controls Punjab's public wealth, and who answers when it is sold? A proposed law to turn unused government land and buildings into revenue-generating assets has raised fears that, in the name of economic gains, public property and decision-making could be drawn away from local institutions and concentrated in the hands of provincial bureaucrats.

The Punjab government has introduced the Asset Management Authority of Punjab Bill 2026 in the provincial assembly, proposing a body empowered to identify, value, lease, sell and develop public assets through joint ventures and public-private partnerships. Its jurisdiction would extend beyond provincial departments to autonomous bodies, authorities and local governments.

Economist Khalid Rasool warned that the proposed authority would further centralise powers at the provincial level, undermining the autonomy of local governments and public institutions. He argued that local bodies should retain control over their assets and resources to address the specific development needs of their communities.

He also questioned the authority's bureaucratic composition, saying the absence of adequate representation from elected representatives, the provincial cabinet and local governments would weaken independent oversight. Its extensive powers to obtain property records and issue directions to public institutions, he added, lack clear limitations and an effective mechanism for appeal.

Rasool further questioned the Chief Minister's discretion in appointing the managing director, arguing that recruitment should follow an open, merit-based process. Citing Punjab's experience with more than 50 management companies established during Shehbaz Sharif's tenure, he warned that transferring responsibilities and resources to another centralised body could invite similar allegations of favouritism, nepotism and corruption.

"Strengthening existing departments and devolving powers to local governments would be a more sustainable approach," maintained Rasool.

Advocate Azhar Siddique also warned that the proposed legislation could threaten fundamental rights, public ownership and accountability by allowing the authority to take control of properties belonging to local governments and autonomous institutions without adequate consent.

He raised concerns under Articles 4, 9, 10A, 23, 24, 25 and 140A of the Constitution, arguing that provisions affecting forests, wildlife sanctuaries, parks and Waqf properties could undermine existing legal protections. He also criticised Section 40, which requires the authority's prior approval before legal proceedings can be initiated against its officials, saying it could weaken independent accountability.

Siddique further questioned whether provisions for direct contracting, unsolicited investment proposals and concessions would ensure transparent transactions. He warned that sweeping eviction powers and restrictions on judicial intervention could also compromise citizens' rights and access to justice.

Under the proposed financial arrangement, 98 per cent of net proceeds from asset sales and projects would go into the Punjab Provincial Consolidated Fund, while the authority would retain two per cent for administrative expenses. Its accounts would be audited annually by the Auditor General of Pakistan and a chartered accountant.

The concerns emerge as Punjab faces substantial financial obligations. The provincial budget for 2026-27 stands at Rs5,903 billion, including Rs752 billion for development spending, while the government has set a cash surplus target of Rs910 billion.

Punjab Finance Minister Mian Mujtaba Shujaur Rehman has said the authority is intended to improve the utilisation of public assets, generate additional revenue and direct resources towards development. However, the bill does not specify the total value of provincial assets or establish a revenue target from their commercialisation.

The central question, critics argue, is whether generating revenue from public property can be achieved without weakening institutional autonomy, public ownership and accountability. The success of the proposed authority will ultimately depend not only on how much money it generates, but also on who controls these assets and who has the power to hold that authority accountable.

article_html:
LAHORE:

Who controls Punjab's public wealth, and who answers when it is sold? A proposed law to turn unused government land and buildings into revenue-generating assets has raised fears that, in the name of economic gains, public property and decision-making could be drawn away from local institutions and concentrated in the hands of provincial bureaucrats.

The Punjab government has introduced the Asset Management Authority of Punjab Bill 2026 in the provincial assembly, proposing a body empowered to identify, value, lease, sell and develop public assets through joint ventures and public-private partnerships. Its jurisdiction would extend beyond provincial departments to autonomous bodies, authorities and local governments.

Economist Khalid Rasool warned that the proposed authority would further centralise powers at the provincial level, undermining the autonomy of local governments and public institutions. He argued that local bodies should retain control over their assets and resources to address the specific development needs of their communities.

He also questioned the authority's bureaucratic composition, saying the absence of adequate representation from elected representatives, the provincial cabinet and local governments would weaken independent oversight. Its extensive powers to obtain property records and issue directions to public institutions, he added, lack clear limitations and an effective mechanism for appeal.

Rasool further questioned the Chief Minister's discretion in appointing the managing director, arguing that recruitment should follow an open, merit-based process. Citing Punjab's experience with more than 50 management companies established during Shehbaz Sharif's tenure, he warned that transferring responsibilities and resources to another centralised body could invite similar allegations of favouritism, nepotism and corruption.

"Strengthening existing departments and devolving powers to local governments would be a more sustainable approach," maintained Rasool.

Advocate Azhar Siddique also warned that the proposed legislation could threaten fundamental rights, public ownership and accountability by allowing the authority to take control of properties belonging to local governments and autonomous institutions without adequate consent.

He raised concerns under Articles 4, 9, 10A, 23, 24, 25 and 140A of the Constitution, arguing that provisions affecting forests, wildlife sanctuaries, parks and Waqf properties could undermine existing legal protections. He also criticised Section 40, which requires the authority's prior approval before legal proceedings can be initiated against its officials, saying it could weaken independent accountability.

Siddique further questioned whether provisions for direct contracting, unsolicited investment proposals and concessions would ensure transparent transactions. He warned that sweeping eviction powers and restrictions on judicial intervention could also compromise citizens' rights and access to justice.

Under the proposed financial arrangement, 98 per cent of net proceeds from asset sales and projects would go into the Punjab Provincial Consolidated Fund, while the authority would retain two per cent for administrative expenses. Its accounts would be audited annually by the Auditor General of Pakistan and a chartered accountant.

The concerns emerge as Punjab faces substantial financial obligations. The provincial budget for 2026-27 stands at Rs5,903 billion, including Rs752 billion for development spending, while the government has set a cash surplus target of Rs910 billion.

Punjab Finance Minister Mian Mujtaba Shujaur Rehman has said the authority is intended to improve the utilisation of public assets, generate additional revenue and direct resources towards development. However, the bill does not specify the total value of provincial assets or establish a revenue target from their commercialisation.

The central question, critics argue, is whether generating revenue from public property can be achieved without weakening institutional autonomy, public ownership and accountability. The success of the proposed authority will ultimately depend not only on how much money it generates, but also on who controls these assets and who has the power to hold that authority accountable.

headline: Theft of steel bars leaves infrastructure vulnerable to collapse
description: 50 bridges, flyovers and underpasses have been damaged due to vandalism
author: Syed Ashraf Ali
article_text:
Theft of steel reinforcement bars has weakened more than 50 bridges, flyovers and underpasses across Karachi, raising fears of structural failure. Despite repeated thefts, police have failed to stop the damage, while delayed repairs by civic agencies continue to put public safety at risk.

According to an Express Tribune survey, theft of steel bars from pillars, foundations and protective walls has continued for months. After targeting manhole covers, railings around parks and playgrounds, and pedestrian bridges, suspected drug addicts have increasingly turned to major road infrastructure, threatening public safety.

Dhobi Ghat Bridge, Miranaka Bridge and Natha Khan Bridge are among the structures reportedly in a dilapidated condition. Residents and local representatives fear that the weakened bridges may be unable to withstand increased traffic loads.

Drug addiction and related thefts have increased in Karachi over the past two decades, with manhole cover thefts becoming routine. Several people, including children, have been killed or injured after falling into uncovered manholes. Although the Karachi Water and Sewerage Corporation replaces stolen covers, delays of three to four days can leave pedestrians at risk.

Despite repeated fatalities, the Sindh government and police have yet to establish a comprehensive rehabilitation strategy or take sustained action against drug dealers. Meanwhile, an Express Tribune survey found damage to nearly all city bridges, flyovers and underpasses, particularly those over the Lyari and Malir rivers and railway tracks, where limited public movement, inadequate patrols and a lack of surveillance cameras facilitate steel thefts.

Thefts have also occurred on busy thoroughfares despite police patrols and surveillance cameras. Steel reinforcement bars have been removed from pillars, while protective posts and reinforcement have been stolen from Jersey barriers installed to safeguard pedestrians.

Last month, damage to the foundations of Teen Hatti Bridge came to light after steel bars were stolen from its pillars and walls. Following media reports, the Karachi Metropolitan Corporation (KMC) carried out repairs. The corporation has also repaired Liaquatabad, Gharibabad and Nazimabad underpasses and Golimar Bridge. However, several other structures remain unrepaired.

Among those reported to be in particularly poor condition are Miranaka and Dhobi Ghat bridges over the Lyari River, Shah Faisal Colony Bridge over the Malir River, and Natha Khan and Lilly bridges over railway tracks. Sher Shah and Younas Abad flyovers have also sustained considerable damage. At several locations, concrete has been broken away and protective walls damaged, increasing the risk of accidents.

Babu Lasi, general secretary of the Golimar Social Welfare Organisation, said suspected drug addicts had broken the protective walls of Love Lane Bridge over the Lyari River and stolen steel bars, creating a risk of pedestrians, particularly children, falling from the bridge.

He said the walls had since been repaired using funds from an MNA. However, Miranaka and Dhobi Ghat bridges remained in poor condition, with steel bars missing from their foundations and protective walls. Despite repeated complaints to the relevant civic authorities, repairs had yet to begin.

Lasi urged the government to establish a long-term rehabilitation programme for drug addicts and take effective measures to protect public infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Keamari police zone said pickets had been established around the Lyari Expressway, including Miranaka, Jahanabad and Golimar, to curb activities involving drug addicts. Over the past six months, police had conducted multiple operations, referring more than 1,000 individuals to welfare organisations for treatment and rehabilitation while arresting hundreds of suspected drug dealers.

KMC Chief Engineer Ishrat Rehan said repair proposals for Miranaka, Dhobi Ghat and Natha Khan bridges, along with other damaged structures, had been submitted. "Construction work would begin as soon as funds become available," he added.

Among those reported to be in particularly poor condition are Miranaka and Dhobi Ghat bridges over the Lyari River, Shah Faisal Colony Bridge over the Malir River, and Natha Khan and Lilly bridges over railway tracks. Sher Shah and Younas Abad flyovers have also sustained considerable damage. At several locations, concrete has been broken away and protective walls damaged, increasing the risk of accidents.

Babu Lasi, general secretary of the Golimar Social Welfare Organisation, said suspected drug addicts had broken the protective walls of Love Lane Bridge over the Lyari River and stolen steel bars, creating a risk of pedestrians, particularly children, falling from the bridge.

He said the walls had since been repaired using funds from an MNA. However, Miranaka and Dhobi Ghat bridges remained in poor condition, with steel bars missing from their foundations and protective walls. Despite repeated complaints to the relevant civic authorities, repairs had yet to begin.
Lasi urged the government to establish a long-term rehabilitation programme for drug addicts and take effective measures to protect public infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Keamari police zone said pickets had been established around the Lyari Expressway, including Miranaka, Jahanabad and Golimar, to curb activities involving drug addicts. Over the past six months, police had conducted multiple operations, referring more than 1,000 individuals to welfare organisations for treatment and rehabilitation while arresting hundreds of suspected drug dealers.

KMC Chief Engineer Ishrat Rehan said repair proposals for Miranaka, Dhobi Ghat and Natha Khan bridges, along with other damaged structures, had been submitted. "Construction work would begin as soon as funds become available," he added.

headline: Gulf Arab states approve military command headquarters in Kuwait
description: No further details on the ​headquarters, forces to be deployed are immediately available
author: Reuters
article_text:
The six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states on Tuesday approved the establishment of an ​advanced headquarters for their Unified Military Command ‌in Kuwait and the deployment of "appropriate" forces to it, the GCC Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said.

Albudaiwi said the decision was approved during the 23rd session of the Joint Defence Council, held in Bahrain's capital, Manama, according to a statement issued by the bloc.

The GCC secretary-general stressed that GCC leaders attach great importance to joint military cooperation, recognising the role of their armed forces in safeguarding regional security, stability and sovereignty.

Albudaiwi said the meeting's agenda included several significant decisions aimed at expanding military cooperation and advancing defence integration among member states, without providing further details.

The meeting was chaired by Bahrain's Minister of Defence Affairs Lt Gen Abdullah bin Hassan Al Nuaimi, with the participation of defence ministers from the five other member states of the bloc.

No further details on the ​headquarters or the forces to be deployed ​were immediately available.

The meeting came amid heightened regional tensions, including Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, concerns over renewed military confrontation between the US and Iran, and continued disruptions to maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

The war has disrupted air travel and shipping, and raised ⁠concerns ​over the security of the ​region's vital oil and gas exports.

The GCC established its Unified Military Command ​at a summit in Kuwait in December 2013 to ‌plan ⁠and manage joint military operations and strengthen member states' defence capabilities against potential threats to their territory, airspace, waters and interests.

The latest decision follows an October 29 meeting of GCC armed forces chiefs of staff in Manama, where military leaders discussed strengthening defence cooperation and coordination in response to regional security challenges.

The GCC, established in 1981, is a six-member regional organisation comprising Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman, aimed at promoting political, economic and security cooperation.

headline: Shah Mahmood rushed to Punjab Institute of Cardiology after reported prison collapse
description: Family seeks comprehensive medical assessment, including CT scan
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Senior PTI leader Shah Mahmood Qureshi was on Tuesday transferred to Lahore's Punjab Institute of Cardiology (PIC) after reportedly collapsing inside Kot Lakhpat jail, prompting his family to seek urgent medical investigations and treatment.

The former foreign minister's lawyer Rana Mudassar Umar confirmed the transfer on Tuesday, saying Qureshi had fainted and suffered a fall a few days earlier. His family has separately called for a CT scan and dental treatment, while the PTI's core committee has urged authorities to ensure his complete medical examination.

Qureshi is currently being kept under observation for 24 hours, after which doctors will decide whether he needs to be admitted to the hospital.

His counsel said Qureshi was taken to PIC today after he fainted and suffered a fall a few days ago, adding that an application had been in the anti-terrorism court but the issue was delayed due to holidays.

He added that Qureshi was being kept under observation for 24 hours, “after which it will be decided whether he has to be admitted to the hospital”.

The hospital transfer comes after repeated expressions of concern by Qureshi's family over his condition in prison. Last week, his daughter Meher Bano said in a post on X that she had learnt about her father's fall from family members who met him at Kot Lakhpat jail.

“Three-and-a-half years ago a hale and hearty lion heart was sent to jail on trumped-up charges … For over two years, he has been in Kot Lakhpat jail now facing ludicrous and false charges relating to May 9. He has been acquitted multiple times but [remains] behind bars due to the government’s mala fides,” she alleged.

Qureshi's son, Zain, said on Wednesday that his father had told him during a jail meeting that he collapsed while walking inside his barracks.

Seeking further medical intervention, he urged the prison authorities to arrange a CT scan and specialised dental treatment.

“I request the prison authorities to immediately arrange for a CT scan so that his health condition can be thoroughly assessed. Furthermore, he should be taken to a qualified dentist for the treatment of a cracked tooth,” he said on X.

The PTI's core committee had also raised concerns over Qureshi's condition at a meeting on November 6, expressing alarm over his fall and its possible impact on his health.

It called on the relevant courts, the government and the prison administration to ensure his immediate transfer to a hospital, followed by a complete medical examination and necessary treatment.

The PTI vice-president is facing several charges related to the May 9, 2023 riots. In July 2024, he was indicted by an anti-terrorism court in a case concerning the alleged attack and arson at Shadman police station.

Previously held at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi, Qureshi was moved to Kot Lakhpat Jail last year due to logistical concerns over frequent court appearances in Lahore.

Earlier this year, an anti-terrorism court acquitted Qureshi in the May 9 case involving the arson of police vehicles in Mughalpura. However, he remains in jail in connection with other cases, including those related to rioting.

headline: 13 Pakistanis dead in Greek detention since 2000: report
description: Research draws attention to links between repressive policing, violence against racialised people in Greece
author: Anadolu Agency
article_text:
Research published by the University of Oxford on Tuesday found that 13 Pakistani nationals had died in Greek detention since 2000.

The archive, published on Detention Landscapes in English, Greek and Arabic, adds to long-standing efforts elsewhere to document border and immigration control-related deaths where reliable government data is not available.

The report said that at least 112 foreign nationals in total had died in police and immigration detention facilities in Greece since 2000, with authorities failing to maintain a reliable public record of the deaths.

According to the study, Pakistani and Albanian nationals accounted for the largest identified groups by nationality, with 13 deaths each. The nationality of 32 individuals was not specified.

The findings, based on police data obtained through Freedom of Information requests, reports by international monitoring bodies, media archives and interviews with formerly detained people, document deaths in police stations and immigration detention facilities across the country.

Since Greece opened its first pre-removal detention centre in 2012, at least 27 deaths have been reported in these facilities, according to the research.

Researchers said Greek authorities do not routinely publish statistics on the number of foreign nationals who die in custody, their identities, the locations of their deaths or the circumstances surrounding them.

The study found that most of the documented deaths involved men, with 82 male victims, while four involved women. The gender of 26 individuals was not recorded.

Of the 70 people whose ages were known, the median age was 33.5, while 45 were under 40.

Suicide was the most frequently recorded cause of death in official police or government sources, accounting for 44 cases, followed by pathological causes in 20 cases. Authorities did not report a cause of death in 36 cases.

Medical neglect, physical abuse

Non-governmental sources also raised concerns about medical neglect and physical abuse in some cases, the report said.

Researchers highlighted significant gaps in information about people who died in state custody, saying basic details about their identities and the circumstances of their deaths remained undocumented even though they had been held by state authorities.

Media reports on deaths in detention were generally limited to brief accounts reproducing information provided by police, with little information about the individuals or the circumstances surrounding their deaths. Accounts from families, friends and fellow detainees were also frequently missing.

The research also draws attention to links between restrictive immigration policies, violence against racialised people and repressive policing in Greek society.

headline: Uzma moves SC for early hearing of Imran's medical transfer case
description: Urges court to appoint local commission amid SC, FCC jurisdiction dispute
author: Hasnaat Maik
article_text:
As neither the Supreme Court nor the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) has fixed a date for hearing the matter concerning former prime minister Imran Khan's transfer from Adiala jail to a private medical facility, an application was filed in the Supreme Court on Tuesday on behalf of his sister, Uzma Khan, seeking early hearing of the case.

Uzma, who has herself been detained under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) at Kot Lakhpat Jail, moved an application requesting the apex court to urgently take up the matter concerning Imran's transfer from Adiala jail to Shifa International Hospital in compliance with its August 18 order.

Earlier, Senator Mashal Yousafzai had also filed an application seeking early hearing of the case.

Uzma had already filed a contempt petition against the prime minister and other executive authorities over their alleged failure to implement the August 18 order.

The latest application also urged the court to depute one of its officers or appoint a local commission to oversee Imran's transfer to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination.

Explaining the urgency, the applicant submitted that, according to media reports, the PTI founder's blood pressure had recently risen to 192, raising serious concerns about his health.

"If an early hearing of this matter is not granted, the applicant's and Imran guaranteed rights will continue to be prejudiced; in particular, his fundamental right to health and well-being, access to medical advice and facilities as well as to members of his family will continue to be violated.”

The application further stated: "The material showing the precarious state of his health and the widespread public concern about it has already been filed with the petition.”

The SC was also requested to fix the main case for hearing next week.

On September 14, the FCC had summoned the record of the case concerning Imran's health from the SC.

Subsequently, on September 16, a three-member bench headed by Justice Shahid Waheed raised questions about the FCC's order. During the hearing, Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Awan sought three weeks to assist the SC in the matter.

Despite two months having passed, the SC has not fixed the matter for hearing. The FCC, meanwhile, listed the three-prisoners case in which it had sought the record of Imran's health-related case.

A lawyer believes that the matter's continued absence from the cause lists of both courts suggests there may be an informal understanding between the SC and the FCC.

He said that instead of allowing the matter to linger, the jurisdictional question between the two apex courts needed to be resolved.

The latest application also urged the court to depute one of its officers or appoint a local commission to oversee Imran's transfer to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination.

Explaining the urgency, the applicant submitted that, according to media reports, the PTI founder's blood pressure had recently risen to 192, raising serious concerns about his health.

"If an early hearing of this matter is not granted, the applicant's and Imran guaranteed rights will continue to be prejudiced; in particular, his fundamental right to health and well-being, access to medical advice and facilities as well as to members of his family will continue to be violated.”

The application further stated: "The material showing the precarious state of his health and the widespread public concern about it has already been filed with the petition.”

The SC was also requested to fix the main case for hearing next week.

On September 14, the FCC had summoned the record of the case concerning Imran's health from the SC.

Subsequently, on September 16, a three-member bench headed by Justice Shahid Waheed raised questions about the FCC's order. During the hearing, Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Awan sought three weeks to assist the SC in the matter.

Despite two months having passed, the SC has not fixed the matter for hearing. The FCC, meanwhile, listed the three-prisoners case in which it had sought the record of Imran's health-related case.

A lawyer believes that the matter's continued absence from the cause lists of both courts suggests there may be an informal understanding between the SC and the FCC.

He said that instead of allowing the matter to linger, the jurisdictional question between the two apex courts needed to be resolved.

headline: Pakistan-Sri Lanka second Test moved from Lahore to Rawalpindi
description: PCB shifts November 17-21 fixture amid rising smog level in Lahore
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
PCB shifts November 17-21 fixture amid rising smog level in Lahore

Pakistan's second Test against Sri Lanka has been relocated from Lahore to Rawalpindi because of rising smog levels in the provincial capital, the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) said on Tuesday.

The match, originally scheduled to take place at Lahore's Gaddafi Stadium from November 17 to 21, will now be played at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium over the same dates.

A PCB spokesperson confirmed the venue change, saying the decision was taken in view of prevailing weather conditions and increasing smog levels in Lahore.

The relocation is aimed at addressing concerns surrounding the deteriorating environmental conditions in Lahore, where seasonal smog has increasingly become a challenge during the winter months.

Lahore has regularly experienced severe air pollution during the winter season, when cooler temperatures, stagnant atmospheric conditions and emissions from vehicles and industrial activity contribute to the accumulation of smog. Poor air quality can pose health concerns for players, officials, support staff and spectators, particularly during prolonged outdoor sporting events.

The first Test between the two nations is in operation at the Pindi Stadium.

headline: Petrol drops by Rs8, diesel by Rs7 for Nov 11
description: Petrol price decreases to Rs338 per litre, while HSD will cost Rs371 under daily price mechanism
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The federal government on Tuesday slashed the price of petrol by Rs8 per litre and that of high-speed diesel (HSD) by Rs7 per litre for November 11.

According to a notification issued by the Petroleum Division, the price of petrol was fixed at Rs338 per litre, while HSD would cost Rs371 per litre for Wednesday.

The revision comes after the government slashed the price of petrol by Rs6.59 per litre and that of HSD by Rs4.25 per litre from November 7 to November 10.

On November 2, the government announced that oil refineries would bear a burden of Rs15 billion per month, which would allow petrol to be sold Rs15 cheaper than it was in the global market amid the US-Israeli war on Iran.

On July 17, the government announced a new pricing mechanism under which petroleum product prices would be reviewed and notified daily, replacing the weekly pricing mechanism, as renewed tensions between the United States and Iran continued to drive volatility in global oil markets and raise concerns over fuel supplies.

On September 13, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a special relief scheme offering Rs100 per litre off petrol for motorcycles, three-wheeler rickshaws and cars with engines up to 800cc, in an attempt to shield lower-income consumers from the impact of rising petroleum prices.

Under the proposal, an estimated 11.8 million beneficiaries would be covered. Around 10 million two-wheeler users and 800,000 three-wheeler users would be entitled to relief on 20 litres of fuel per month, translating into a maximum monthly benefit of Rs2,000 per beneficiary.

Another one million users of cars up to 800cc would receive relief on 30 litres per month, providing them with a maximum benefit of Rs3,000 each.

On Sept 17, the government reintroduced austerity and fuel conservation measures amid rising fuel prices, tightening business operating hours and restricting public events.

Under the measures, notified with immediate effect, shops, markets, shopping malls, bazaars, departmental stores, grocery stores, general stores and kiryana shops would close by 9pm throughout the week, according to a notification issued by the Cabinet Division.

Marriage halls, marquees and other commercial venues hosting festive events would close by 10pm, while restaurants, cafes, eateries, food outlets and standalone fruit and vegetable shops would be allowed to operate until 11pm. Takeaway and home delivery services would remain exempt from the timing restrictions.

headline: NAB issues second notice to JUI-F chief's son over alleged 'illegal appointments' in Pakistan Post
description: Asad Mahmood directed to appear in person at 11am on November 13
author: AAMIR ILAYS RANA
article_text:
The National Accountability Bureau (NAB) on Tuesday issued a second call-up notice to the son of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, Asad Mahmood, directing him to appear before the anti-graft watchdog on November 13 in an inquiry into alleged illegal appointments in the Pakistan Post Office Department (PPOD).

NAB Rawalpindi is conducting an inquiry against officials and employees of the PPOD and others over allegations of illegal recruitment.

Mahmood, who served as federal minister for communications and postal services from 2022 to 2023, was summoned in connection with the alleged appointments made during his tenure.

Mahmood was required to appear before NAB on November 10 but failed to do so and instead had submitted a written response through his lawyer.

NAB officials declared his response unsatisfactory and issued a fresh notice, directing him to appear in person at 11am on Friday.

The notice warned that failure to appear could lead to legal proceedings under Section 31 of the National Accountability Ordinance, 1999.

NAB had earlier summoned Rehman's son on November 5 over alleged irregularities in the appointments at the PPOD during his tenure.

According to the earlier NAB notice, the Establishment Division had authorised recruitment against 3,938 posts at the Pakistan Post Office, but 4,252 people were allegedly appointed. The inquiry has also flagged appointments against 2,646 abolished posts, allegedly in violation of cabinet committee directives.

NAB maintains that despite recommendations for contractual recruitment through a testing agency, a large number of permanent appointments were made, potentially placing an additional financial burden on the department.

headline: JI, govt agree on draft outlines for petroleum levy relief
description: Liaquat Baloch warns JI may resume its long march if talks with the government fail to produce a concrete outcome
author: Web Desk
article_text:
The Jamaat-e-Islami (JI) on Tuesday said it had agreed with the government on the broad outlines of an agreement to extend petroleum-related relief to consumers, but warned it could resume its long march if the negotiations failed to produce a concrete outcome on its demand for abolishing the petroleum levy.

The government and JI held a 10th round of talks on the petroleum levy, with both sides agreeing on the need to provide relief to consumers, particularly low-income households, while discussions on a phased reduction of the levy also came under discussion.

Speaking at a press conference after the 10th round of talks with the government committee, JI deputy chief Liaquat Baloch said the two sides had agreed on the need to expand the existing relief measures, while the government would consult the International Monetary Fund (IMF) on continuing the relief.

He said providing relief to the public remained the foremost concern during the negotiations and that the government had acknowledged difficulties in the supply of petroleum products due to the global situation.

Baloch said JI had proposed including vehicles with engines of up to 1,000cc and the agricultural sector in the relief scheme.

He said the government had also acknowledged that JI's demand for abolishing the petroleum levy was legitimate.

“Our demand is that the levy should be abolished immediately and the public should be given clear relief,” he said, criticising the government for being unwilling to cut its luxuries and putting the burden of the Federal Board of Revenue's (FBR) failures on consumers.

Baloch said the two sides had agreed on the broad outlines of a draft agreement during Tuesday's meeting, with the government expected to share further details in the coming days.

He said that the government had informed the JI delegation that it had started working on a plan to address its revenue requirements and would share a framework for gradually reducing the levy after consultations with the IMF.

He said another meeting was expected on Wednesday or Thursday, while the final decision on the proposed agreement would be taken during a possible meeting between Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and JI chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman.

Following that meeting, the party would decide whether to proceed with its planned long march, he added.

The JI leader claimed that the party's protest had helped halt increases in petroleum prices and secured relief of Rs146 per litre on diesel and Rs120 per litre on petrol.

“The process has now reached the stage of final decisions,” he said.

He said JI remained committed to peaceful political engagement but would withdraw from the negotiations if it found that the government was unwilling to move forward.

“Our only goal is that the people should get relief, that there should be a reduction in production costs, that the economy should run and that people should get employment,” he said, adding that the party's protests and political pressure were aimed at securing relief for the public.

The government also confirmed the talks, with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar holding a follow-up meeting with a JI delegation led by Baloch to continue consultations on petroleum prices and relief for consumers, according to a statement issued by the DPM's Office.

The statement said both sides held constructive discussions on measures to provide relief to consumers, particularly low-income households.

There was broad agreement on the need to address public concerns through continued consultation and cooperation, it added.

Dar welcomed the positive spirit of the engagement and reiterated that the government remained focused on supporting ordinary households amid prevailing economic challenges.

The meeting was attended by Adviser to the Prime Minister on Inter-Provincial Coordination Rana Sanaullah, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Tariq Bajwa, the special secretary of the Petroleum Division, an additional secretary of the Finance Division and JI delegation members Syed Firasat Shah, Nasrullah Randhawa and Inayatullah Khan.

Background

JI’s campaign against the petroleum levy intensified in August, when the party organised demonstrations and sit-ins across the country against rising fuel prices, inflation and what it described as an additional tax burden on consumers. On August 16, JI workers staged sit-ins outside governors’ houses in the provincial capitals, demanding the withdrawal of the levy and a reduction in petrol prices.

The party subsequently expanded its protests to other cities, including Karachi, where it established additional protest camps across Sindh. JI maintained that the government should abolish the levy rather than offer limited reductions in fuel prices.

On September 3, the government and JI agreed to establish technical committees to examine proposals for reducing the petroleum levy and fuel prices. During the first round of negotiations on September 7, the party submitted six proposals to the government, while insisting that its protests would continue until meaningful relief was provided.

However, the negotiations failed to resolve the dispute. On September 12, JI chief announced a long march towards Islamabad for September 20, warning that the party would intensify its campaign if the government did not abolish the levy.

The march began on September 20, with participants travelling from Karachi by train. The caravan moved through Sukkur towards Multan, where Naeem addressed supporters. The march was subsequently suspended after PM Shehbaz telephoned the JI chief and requested that the party postpone its protest to allow further negotiations.

JI agreed to give the government an opportunity for talks but maintained that it had not abandoned its demand. The party’s position was that negotiations and protests could continue simultaneously, with any agreement required to address the complete abolition of the levy.

The JI chief then gave the government 10 days to abolish the petroleum levy and provide meaningful relief to the inflation-hit public, warning that his party would resume its long march towards Islamabad in mid-November if its demands were not met.

“Our demand is that the levy should be abolished immediately and the public should be given clear relief,” he said, criticising the government for being unwilling to cut its luxuries and putting the burden of the Federal Board of Revenue's (FBR) failures on consumers.

Baloch said the two sides had agreed on the broad outlines of a draft agreement during Tuesday's meeting, with the government expected to share further details in the coming days.

He said that the government had informed the JI delegation that it had started working on a plan to address its revenue requirements and would share a framework for gradually reducing the levy after consultations with the IMF.

He said another meeting was expected on Wednesday or Thursday, while the final decision on the proposed agreement would be taken during a possible meeting between Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and JI chief Hafiz Naeemur Rehman.

Following that meeting, the party would decide whether to proceed with its planned long march, he added.

The JI leader claimed that the party's protest had helped halt increases in petroleum prices and secured relief of Rs146 per litre on diesel and Rs120 per litre on petrol.

“The process has now reached the stage of final decisions,” he said.

He said JI remained committed to peaceful political engagement but would withdraw from the negotiations if it found that the government was unwilling to move forward.

“Our only goal is that the people should get relief, that there should be a reduction in production costs, that the economy should run and that people should get employment,” he said, adding that the party's protests and political pressure were aimed at securing relief for the public.

The government also confirmed the talks, with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar holding a follow-up meeting with a JI delegation led by Baloch to continue consultations on petroleum prices and relief for consumers, according to a statement issued by the DPM's Office.

The statement said both sides held constructive discussions on measures to provide relief to consumers, particularly low-income households.

There was broad agreement on the need to address public concerns through continued consultation and cooperation, it added.

Dar welcomed the positive spirit of the engagement and reiterated that the government remained focused on supporting ordinary households amid prevailing economic challenges.

The meeting was attended by Adviser to the Prime Minister on Inter-Provincial Coordination Rana Sanaullah, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Tariq Bajwa, the special secretary of the Petroleum Division, an additional secretary of the Finance Division and JI delegation members Syed Firasat Shah, Nasrullah Randhawa and Inayatullah Khan.

Background

JI’s campaign against the petroleum levy intensified in August, when the party organised demonstrations and sit-ins across the country against rising fuel prices, inflation and what it described as an additional tax burden on consumers. On August 16, JI workers staged sit-ins outside governors’ houses in the provincial capitals, demanding the withdrawal of the levy and a reduction in petrol prices.

The party subsequently expanded its protests to other cities, including Karachi, where it established additional protest camps across Sindh. JI maintained that the government should abolish the levy rather than offer limited reductions in fuel prices.

On September 3, the government and JI agreed to establish technical committees to examine proposals for reducing the petroleum levy and fuel prices. During the first round of negotiations on September 7, the party submitted six proposals to the government, while insisting that its protests would continue until meaningful relief was provided.

However, the negotiations failed to resolve the dispute. On September 12, JI chief announced a long march towards Islamabad for September 20, warning that the party would intensify its campaign if the government did not abolish the levy.

The march began on September 20, with participants travelling from Karachi by train. The caravan moved through Sukkur towards Multan, where Naeem addressed supporters. The march was subsequently suspended after PM Shehbaz telephoned the JI chief and requested that the party postpone its protest to allow further negotiations.

JI agreed to give the government an opportunity for talks but maintained that it had not abandoned its demand. The party’s position was that negotiations and protests could continue simultaneously, with any agreement required to address the complete abolition of the levy.

The JI chief then gave the government 10 days to abolish the petroleum levy and provide meaningful relief to the inflation-hit public, warning that his party would resume its long march towards Islamabad in mid-November if its demands were not met.

headline: Digital fame, social shame
description: Digital fame, social shame
author: Muhammad Wajahat Sultan
article_text:
As the TikTok economy has become a sociological phenomenon in our country, it is important to understand the changing contours of social identity, visibility, cultural acceptance, diversified economic performance and platformisation. One side is represented by people who have invested years of their social experience through institutional exposure, education and traditional mechanisms of building social identity and visibility, while the other side represents quick visibility, often without traditionally recognised cognitive skills, and financial success through emerging economic models. The tension between the two is sometimes not about genuine moral disagreement but about the underlying insecurity of not adapting to digital platforms and new identities.

Our society is still at an early stage of accepting new forms of democratisation of economic participation and the possibility of achieving financial independence through the platform economy. Sometimes, this insecurity stems from compromised cultural values, while at other times, it emerges from the importation of a homogeneous, globalised social structure. TikTok and other digital platforms represent a new form of decoupled economies based on platformisation, where people without traditionally established or celebrated norms of intelligence or intellect can mainstream their forms of social performance and intersect them with economic outcomes.

Pakistani society accepts the same content of dramas and films, but its becomes difficult to accept the similar forms of expression that emerge from people who lack conventional educational or intellectual credentials. What is celebrated on television or in films can suddenly become a source of embarrassment when ordinary individuals perform it on digital platforms and earn a living from it. If the very same thing is opted for by a third party or decentralised as a source of income or content diversification, it becomes a source of disgrace to our culture. Apparently, no TikTokker has mainstreamed content involving objectionable morality, such as nudity or compromised bodily exposure. Then why do people in Pakistan associate all evil and bad things with TikTokkers?

There are mainly two reasons. First, there is an unconscious lack of acceptance of new forms of earning potential through digital platforms, leading to unbearable stress and anxiety among people who unintentionally consider themselves incapable of achieving so much through these new money-making platforms. Second, there is cultural rigidity in associating everything with good and bad. If something is not introduced through socially constructed norms, a long-term path to gaining visibility and hard work, it becomes unacceptable from a moral standpoint because, culturally, we have never been exposed to instant, short-term and alternative means of gaining visibility.

In the coming days, the traditional sense of the American Dream will become less relevant. This does not mean that we should abandon established educational processes. It means that economic activity and performance have diversified. Diversification and adaptation are always difficult. The transition and social change require time to build new momentum towards accepting emerging norms.

The idea of declining children's grooming and future prospects is not inherently connected to the TikTok economy or digital platforms. Social institutions such as family, religion and schools should accordingly change their approach to raising children, with careful consideration of changing economies and their modes of performance. It is always easy, in times of social change, to disassociate the failures of social institutions in performing their manifest and latent functions and diffuse this failure onto new forms of emerging institutions. It is time for our social institutions to reconsider new designs or new forms of social norms and values to develop our coming generations, both as individuals and in their relationships with others.

headline: The uniting opposition
description: The uniting opposition
author: editorial
article_text:
New political realignments are being envisaged to push a strong anti-government agenda. JUI-F is at the vanguard of efforts to build a strong narrative. The party, led by Maulana Fazlur Rehman, is reportedly in talks with TTAP, the six-party opposition alliance. Mehmood Khan Achakzai's personal efforts to bring the Maulana into the spotlight, along with PTI's support, for a grand coalition of estranged political forces, are now creating ripples. The imposition of governor's rule in K-P has provided a common denominator for the opposition forces that had thus far remained directionless. It had failed to devise a formidable strategy on issues related to the release of political prisoners as well as the controversial constitutional amendments that have undermined the functioning of state institutions.

Rehman has lately been speaking out against the government, expressing his displeasure with policies that have adversely affected two restive provinces. The deteriorating law and order situation in Balochistan, the impasse in K-P and the discord among political parties over the creation of more provinces are simmering as emerging agendas for the opposition, and it remains to be seen what effective course of action is adopted. PTI's inability to bring people onto the streets and play a role in the parliament have presented the JUI-F with an opportunity to take the lead. The Maulana has been quick to seize that opportunity, as is evident from his current critical discourse, providing new momentum to the opposition.

The die, however, is yet to be cast. The opposition parties must move beyond rhetoric and come up with a narrative that appeals to the electorate as a viable way out of the crisis. Addressing political instability, the economic downturn and constitutional lacunae, while restoring the balance of power in statecraft by empowering the judiciary and parliament to act free from executive interference, will be uphill tasks. With talks between the government and the opposition conventionally ending in a deadlock, the way forward for the opposition is to adopt a realistic approach and focus on issue-oriented politics rather than knee-jerk reactions.

headline: Climate justice for Pakistan
description: Pakistan's negotiating priorities are clear
author: editorial
article_text:
COP31 has opened in Antalya with the same familiar and dispiriting contest over money. The UN Secretary-General has urged leaders to "get serious" about a crisis that is no longer a forecast but a daily emergency. Yet, developing nations have had to fight just to put climate finance on the official agenda. For countries like Pakistan, this is not just a diplomatic spectacle. It is a matter of survival.

Pakistan has a negligible carbon footprint - it contributes less than 1% of global emissions - but ranks among the 10 most climate-vulnerable countries, exposed to heatwaves, extreme monsoons and accelerating glacial melt. The 2022 super-floods submerged a third of the country, affected 33 million people and caused over $30 billion in damage. Islamabad now estimates that meeting its climate commitments will require $565 billion by 2035. Where that money will come from is anyone's guess, though self-financing is not a real option - more than 60% of revenues are currently consumed by debt servicing alone.

Pakistan's negotiating priorities are clear - accessible adaptation finance, predictable grant-based loss-and-damage support, and international recognition of threats, including mountain climate risks. As things stand, the Loss and Damage Fund is still embarrassingly small - $342 million available against $2.8 billion in requests, with Pakistan's own $58 million in proposals receiving no allocation.

Experts have suggested that Pakistan build a 'mountain coalition' with countries such as Nepal, Bhutan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan to demand glacier monitoring, early-warning systems and resilient infrastructure. Islamabad should also use ties with China and G77 countries to lobby for more grant-based finance options that will not push affected countries further into debt. And though we can't give much in return, we can at least offer to try improving domestic transparency for donors' funds - though that may be an even more difficult task.

headline: Classroom predators
description: Classroom predators
author: editorial
article_text:
The rising incidence of sexual violence in Pakistan is symptomatic of a society where impunity and institutional negligence continue to endanger women and children. That the perpetrators are sometimes individuals entrusted with the protection and education of young people makes the situation even more disturbing. The alleged rape of a 17-year-old student by the principal of a private college in Bahawalpur district illustrates the dangers of unchecked authority within educational institutions. The victim's father reportedly faced resistance from members of his biradari when he sought to approach the police, reflecting how communal pressures continue to obstruct the pursuit of justice.

The authority exercised by teachers and administrators carries an obligation of care that cannot be compromised. Yet educational institutions frequently operate without meaningful oversight or enforceable child protection protocols. Students are expected to respect and obey those in authority, while questioning their conduct can carry academic and social consequences. This unequal relationship creates opportunities for exploitation, particularly when institutions are more concerned with protecting their reputations than investigating misconduct. There is also a larger failure of the criminal justice system. Pakistan has repeatedly introduced legal measures to address sexual violence, but the gulf between legislation and enforcement remains enormous. The resulting lack of accountability discourages reporting and reinforces the belief that influence can prevail over justice. In cases involving minors, these failures are particularly indefensible. Sexual violence is a criminal offence, not a family dispute to be settled through negotiation or social pressure.

The Bahawalpur allegations demand a prompt, impartial investigation and appropriate action against anyone found responsible. But justice in one case cannot compensate for systemic neglect. Above all, the culture of silence surrounding sexual violence must be confronted. An education system that cannot protect students from abuse within its own institutions is failing in one of its most fundamental responsibilities.

headline: Rice straw can yield clean energy rather than smog
description: Straw burning has become major environmental issue as it not only pollutes environment but also degrades soil ecology
author: Web Desk
article_text:
Pakistan is the tenth largest rice producer in the world and the fourth largest exporter. According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (2024-2025), Pakistan produced more than 9.8 million tonnes of rice grain, while around 13 million tonnes of rice straw was generated when harvested manually or by machines. However, rice straw is currently underutilised because of its low nutritional value and high percentage of silica, making it unsuitable for animal feed. Rice straw is burnt due to no commercial value and due to constraints in collection of straw from field because of high associated costs or time constraints issues for the next crop sowing. Rice straw is sometimes fired for household heating or for cooking in rural areas.

In recent years, straw burning has become a major environmental issue as it not only pollutes the environment but also degrades the soil ecology, affecting the nutrient availability in soil. Intensive rice straw burning occurs within 2 to 4 weeks (mid of October to mid of November) in Pakistan. The burning of rice straw creates various environmental problems, including high GHGs emissions, aerosol particles, such as coarse dust particles (PM10) and fine particles (PM2.5), and toxic gases, such as carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Smog formation occurs due to high amounts of VOCs and nitrogen oxides, which react in the presence of sunlight to form ground-level ozone, which can affect weather conditions. This can further exacerbates environmental conditions when there is no rain during these conditions, resulting in heavy smog.

The world is moving toward a bio circular economy, which is a closed-loop system that replaces fossil fuel-based products with renewable, bio-based materials, primarily from agricultural, forestry, and marine waste, and then cycles these materials back into the economy to minimise waste and pollution. It is a shift towards a nature-powered economy that aims to regenerate natural systems by using natural capital, thereby reducing dependence on non-renewable resources and supporting sustainable well-being.

Pakistan is burning valuable crop residues, such as rice straw, to convert them into issues such as depletion of soil organic matter, environmental pollution, human health toxic smog and fossil fuel energy import bills. According to a study on rice straw valorisation published in the Environmental Science and Pollution Research journal, raw rice straw can be challenging to convert into biogas using specialised microbes. However, this biogas can be purified by removing impurities to produce biomethane, which shares similar applications with natural gas. Biomethane can then be utilised in existing natural gas infrastructure or converted into Liquefied Natural Gas (Bio-LNG). Demand for Bio-LNG is currently soaring, especially as a maritime fuel.

However, lead researcher Muhamamad Abdul Hanan Siddhu notes that approximately 126 m³ of biomethane can be produced per tonne of rice straw through anaerobic digestion, while the biomethane yield can be significantly increased to 205 m³/tonne (63%) of rice straw by developing special techniques and emerging steam explosion pretreatment technology. A subsequent calculation showed that the use of Siddhu's steam explosion pretreatment technology to convert approximately 80% of Pakistan's burned rice straw could produce 2133 million m³ of biomethane or 1.5 million tonnes of Bio-LNG, accounting for 8532 million units of electricity, which could meet the energy demand of roughly 3.7 million households. Steam explosion pretreatment technology is chemical-free, and after harnessing the biomethane potential from rice straw, the residue can be utilised as fertiliser in agricultural production systems to reduce the dependency on expensive imported synthetic inputs and mitigate environmental problems and associated human health risks.

Therefore, the government should promote and support advanced and emerging environment-friendly technologies, such as steam explosion pretreatment, to valorise rice straw into biomethane production and simultaneously mitigate smog, reduce environmental issues and conserve Pakistan's natural resources and its foreign reserves.

According to the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (2024-2025), Pakistan produced more than 9.8 million tonnes of rice grain, while around 13 million tonnes of rice straw was generated when harvested manually or by machines. Rice straw is burnt due to no commercial value and due to constraints in collection of straw from field because of high associated costs or time constraints issues for the next crop sowing. Rice straw is sometimes fired for household heating or for cooking in rural areas.
