headline: Terrorism and the writ of the state
description: Recent acts of terror amplify the scale of the challenge
author: Dr Syed Akhtar Ali Shah
article_text:
Persistent terrorism in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa has inflicted a heavy toll on human life while devastating the region's economy and social fabric - a trend showing no signs of abating. Why does this violence persist despite various counterterrorism strategies and the immense sacrifices of police, security personnel and civilians? The writ of the state cannot be assessed merely by cleared territory or militants killed. The real test is whether citizens can work, travel, attend school, and seek justice without fear.

Recent acts of terror amplify the scale of the challenge. At Speen Mela in Hassan Khel, militants assaulted a police post, martyring Constable Muhammad Jalal and injuring three others. In another incident, five policemen were injured in an attack on the Gumbati checkpost in Bannu. Additional SHO Meera Khan was also shot dead near Miranshah. On October 22, CTD DSP Imranuddin Khan, SHO Afzal Awan and two fellow policemen were martyred in a Karak ambush, which also left two militants dead.

Civilian life remains equally fraught with danger. In one incident, armed militants abducted 17 project and sugar mill workers who remain missing. Such lawlessness carries consequences far beyond the immediate victims; industry cannot flourish where kidnapping and coercion make travel unsafe. Meanwhile, in South Waziristan, a mortar shell struck a house in Toi Khulla, killing three civilians and injuring five. The origin of the shell has yet to be established.

Moreover, in Bannu, a roadside motorcycle bomb exploded near a police patrol, injuring two civilians. Similarly, unverified social media reports indicated that three children were wounded in a quadcopter attack in Bannu on October 23, while a civilian was shot and killed by unidentified gunmen in Bajaur that same day. Together, these unabated acts have intensified the pervasive sense of insecurity.

These incidents and sacrifices, deeply interlinked with the past, require more than just ceremonial tributes; they demand a rigorous review of intelligence, equipment, tactics and operational reinforcements. Against the backdrop of intensified attacks, Malik Khan Marjan, Vice Chairman of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC), has proposed sending a delegation of 15 to 20 authorised tribal elders to Afghanistan to negotiate with the TTP, Hafiz Gul Bahadur's group, and other factions. The urgency behind his appeal is understandable. Communities devastated by decades of violence are desperate to adopt any means necessary to normalise the situation.

However, this proposal is highly questionable and contradicts national counterterrorism policy. Moreover, relying on tribal chiefs to resist organised militant networks - backed by heavy weaponry, funding, territorial networks and ideological command structures - is an exercise in self-deception. The historical record is highly alarming. Data from the South Asia Terrorism Portal reveals that at least 194 tribal elders were killed in 143 separate incidents between 2005 and March 2024. This targeted campaign has severely weakened local resilience and fractured the region's social fabric. Crucially, these figures reflect inherently incomplete media reporting and represent an absolute minimum rather than an exhaustive total.

A significant number of tribal elders who opposed militancy and sided with the government were systematically targeted and killed. For instance, former Senator Malik Faridullah Khan Wazir and two other elders were assassinated in Jandola in 2005. Decades of targeted assassinations, extortion and intimidation have severely eroded traditional authority, silenced local resistance and rendered collective action extremely dangerous. Given this historical pattern, expecting unprotected community representatives to confront highly organised militant groups is an unsound proposition that is unlikely to yield the desired results.

Temporary ceasefires and peace agreements in the past have failed to deliver lasting peace. A government-sponsored tribal jirga helped secure a TTP ceasefire announcement in 2022, but capitulating to their core demands - including the reversal of the former FATA merger - amounted to surrendering the writ of the state, causing the truce to eventually collapse. Any renewed engagement must strictly specify who authorises negotiators, guarantees safety, verifies compliance and ensures that militants cannot exploit pauses to regroup. Crucially, victims, women and affected local communities must not be excluded from decisions that directly shape their security.

Although Malik Marjan's call for dialogue may seem like a personal opinion, given the fact that he is the Vice Chairman of the newly formed ARDC and thus a public face of the government administration, his remarks cannot be easily brushed aside. However, the state policy must remain completely unambiguous and must never abdicate its constitutional responsibilities.

The state's strategy must clearly distinguish between organised militant groups, with their distinct operational patterns, and ordinary criminal gangs. Effective counterterrorism requires integrated intelligence, highly capable Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) units, sound investigations and credible prosecutions. Furthermore, it demands the sustained protection of roads, schools and businesses, alongside - above all - filling the critical gaps in local governance.

Under the 25th Constitutional Amendment, a considerable journey has been undertaken toward administrative, political and judicial integration; however, full financial integration has yet to materialise. Consolidating these reforms requires the provision of finances as mandated by the NFC mechanism under the Constitution of Pakistan.

To properly gauge the security environment, the state must regularly publish verifiable monthly figures on attacks, casualties, kidnappings, extortion cases, investigations and convictions, alongside measurable outcomes for civilian safety. Transparency, accountability and the public welfare - expressed in measurable terms - are indispensable for good governance. While traditional leadership can contribute to localised peace, imagining that vulnerable elders can neutralise sophisticated militant networks misinterprets history and abdicates the core responsibilities of the state. Ultimately, this threat must be tackled directly by the organised force of the state.

Together, these unabated acts have intensified the pervasive sense of insecurity.

These incidents and sacrifices, deeply interlinked with the past, require more than just ceremonial tributes; they demand a rigorous review of intelligence, equipment, tactics and operational reinforcements. Against the backdrop of intensified attacks, Malik Khan Marjan, Vice Chairman of the Area Representative and Development Council (ARDC), has proposed sending a delegation of 15 to 20 authorised tribal elders to Afghanistan to negotiate with the TTP, Hafiz Gul Bahadur's group, and other factions. However, this proposal is highly questionable and contradicts national counterterrorism policy. Moreover, relying on tribal chiefs to resist organised militant networks - backed by heavy weaponry, funding, territorial networks and ideological command structures - is an exercise in self-deception. The historical record is highly alarming. Data from the South Asia Terrorism Portal reveals that at least 194 tribal elders were killed in 143 separate incidents between 2005 and March 2024. This targeted campaign has severely weakened local resilience and fractured the region's social fabric. Crucially, these figures reflect inherently incomplete media reporting and represent an absolute minimum rather than an exhaustive total.

A significant number of tribal elders who opposed militancy and sided with the government were systematically targeted and killed. For instance, former Senator Malik Faridullah Khan Wazir and two other elders were assassinated in Jandola in 2005. Decades of targeted assassinations, extortion and intimidation have severely eroded traditional authority, silenced local resistance and rendered collective action extremely dangerous. Given this historical pattern, expecting unprotected community representatives to confront highly organised militant groups is an unsound proposition that is unlikely to yield the desired results.

Temporary ceasefires and peace agreements in the past have failed to deliver lasting peace. A government-sponsored tribal jirga helped secure a TTP ceasefire announcement in 2022, but capitulating to their core demands - including the reversal of the former FATA merger - amounted to surrendering the writ of the state, causing the truce to eventually collapse. Any renewed engagement must strictly specify who authorises negotiators, guarantees safety, verifies compliance and ensures that militants cannot exploit pauses to regroup. Crucially, victims, women and affected local communities must not be excluded from decisions that directly shape their security.

Although Malik Marjan's call for dialogue may seem like a personal opinion, given the fact that he is the Vice Chairman of the newly formed ARDC and thus a public face of the government administration, his remarks cannot be easily brushed aside. However, the state policy must remain completely unambiguous and must never abdicate its constitutional responsibilities.

The state's strategy must clearly distinguish between organised militant groups, with their distinct operational patterns, and ordinary criminal gangs. Effective counterterrorism requires integrated intelligence, highly capable Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD) units, sound investigations and credible prosecutions. Furthermore, it demands the sustained protection of roads, schools and businesses, alongside - above all - filling the critical gaps in local governance.

Under the 25th Constitutional Amendment, a considerable journey has been undertaken toward administrative, political and judicial integration; however, full financial integration has yet to materialise. Consolidating these reforms requires the provision of finances as mandated by the NFC mechanism under the Constitution of Pakistan.

To properly gauge the security environment, the state must regularly publish verifiable monthly figures on attacks, casualties, kidnappings, extortion cases, investigations and convictions, alongside measurable outcomes for civilian safety. Transparency, accountability and the public welfare - expressed in measurable terms - are indispensable for good governance. While traditional leadership can contribute to localised peace, imagining that vulnerable elders can neutralise sophisticated militant networks misinterprets history and abdicates the core responsibilities of the state. Ultimately, this threat must be tackled directly by the organised force of the state.

headline: Classism - the other face of patriarchy
description: Pakistan needs a more candid structural feminist critique of this convenient omission
author: Dr Rakhshinda Perveen
article_text:
Calling oneself an intersectional feminist is fashionable, even delicious, today. But intersectionality was never meant to be a label; it requires inspecting power, including one's own. How many times such "misadventures" are missed in our feminist activism, I have not counted. As the 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence return (25 November to 10 December 2026), one question keeps circling in my mind: how much of the inequality attributed to patriarchy is also sustained by class privilege and patronage?

Academics, advocates and activists working on gender equality rarely dare to question what class means for their own institutions, movements and professional relationships. Pakistan needs a more candid structural feminist critique of this convenient omission. I understand that asking has a cost; disruption always does. I have been asking since the early 1990s, when I encountered Prof Kimberlé Crenshaw's work on intersectionality.

I have not forgotten what happened when I began teaching gender as visiting faculty at public and private universities more than two decades ago, and when I established AGEHI (Advocates of Gender, Education & Health Information) to demystify gender in Pakistani contexts. AGEHI is also the Urdu word, meaning awareness, knowledge or consciousness. In both spaces, I brought class in rather than reducing gender relations to men versus women. I was diminished and dismissed, and not by ordinary adversaries but by established, elite feminists in academia and activism. I continue to pay a heavy price, and I am glad I persist as a disrupter in its true sense. This piece is not a bid for sympathy or an inventory of grievances. It is an attempt to put on record some inconvenient facets of our feminism.

In Pakistan, class is not simply about income or property. It travels through surnames, biradari, qabila, domicile, accent, degrees, family connections and proximity to influential people. These become informal qualifications, sometimes counting for more than competence. A politically correct surname can do wonders. The right sponsor makes a debatable appointment look decent.

Patriarchy profits from this. A woman's authority is often judged by things unrelated to her work: marital status, family background, social circle, even appearance. She may be qualified and experienced yet expected to prove her acceptability before exercising authority. And if she lacks the right surname, contacts or PR machinery? Dak-khana milta na ho tou, shashka bhi na ho tou? (If she doesn't fit in with the right circle, and isn't even eye candy?) Where does she stand in a system that values social currency over professional substance?

The same fault lines run through donors, diplomats and development actors, who routinely engage with influential surnames and people who get things done through connections. There is operational convenience in this. But what does a donor gain by hiring someone from a marginalised background with no network to smooth the work? Where is the incentive to redistribute access rather than keep negotiating with those who already hold it?

Sometimes the opposite happens: the visibly oppressed are selected for their optics, becoming faces of inclusion and photographs in reports. Visibility is not authority, and representation is not redistribution. Who decides, who controls resources and who receives professional recognition remain separate questions.

The middle class complicates this conversation. Some of us hold professional qualifications, foreign degrees and years of experience in teaching, policy and development. We appear advantaged, and in some respects we are. But we may lack the domicile, connections, sponsors and social acceptability that make privilege count in Pakistan. Class is not simply a line between rich and poor; it is also about who can convert education and experience into recognition and authority.

Nor are the women who do hold that authority necessarily allies. I contest the conjecture that women who have experienced patriarchy automatically become more egalitarian. A woman can challenge male domination and still produce class pyramids, speaking of solidarity while belittling another woman's accent, background or credentials, or championing women's leadership while favouring familiar circles. Many of us have faced not only misogynist men but also women with internalised misogyny, who enjoy every perk and privilege of the system and have never stood with women who are their equals, or even their superiors, in qualification.

Sanitised, donor-approved feminist language does not make the exercise of power feminist; nor does the presence of a woman in a senior position necessarily mean that the hierarchy itself has changed. In Pakistan's civil society and social development sector (many call it business), this gap between language and practice is especially visible.

Organisations advocating gender justice usually have elite boards, opaque recruitment and patronage-based appointments. Women's labour sustains programmes and campaigns while recognition goes elsewhere. Those who question these arrangements risk being labelled difficult or bitter. Empowerment, it seems, is welcome as long as it leaves the distribution of power undisturbed.

Professional exclusion is not the same as the deprivation and violence faced by women living in poverty. Nor does every privileged woman or donor behave alike. The question is why class so often remains outside gender analysis.

Pakistan needs "honest" research (though I wonder how it would be possible) into how class, gender, age, ethnicity and marital status intersect in professional environments. Sex-disaggregated data is a starting point. The harder questions are who gets appointed, whose work is recognised, who holds authority and who receives institutional protection. Donors and development partners should examine their own recruitment, funding and partnership practices rather than rely on familiar elites as intermediaries for inclusion.

The 16 Days should invite scrutiny beyond the vocabulary of empowerment. Who gets into the room, and who decides? Classism is not a side effect of patriarchy; it is one of the ways patriarchy perpetuates its own hierarchies, sometimes with women as gatekeepers and development actors as willing facilitators.

Challenging unequal power while remaining comfortable with the privileges that sustain it is not feminism. And those of us who say so will keep being called, in Kishwar Naheed's phrase, hum gunahgar aurtain.

headline: ‘Hatred should come to an end’: Gohar defends interaction with ex-army chief Bajwa amid criticism
description: Gohar says he exchanged greetings with Bajwa after handshake photo circulated widely on social media
author: Web Desk
article_text:
PTI Chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan on Tuesday defended his brief interaction with former army chief Gen Qamar Javed Bajwa, saying political hostilities should end, and clarified that the two had merely exchanged greetings at a wedding.

A picture of the PTI chairman shaking hands with the former army chief at the function began circulating on social media last week, drawing criticism from PTI supporters and party officials.

They criticised Gohar for interacting with Gen Bajwa, whom they accused of playing a role in the PTI government's ouster in 2022, with some also calling for the PTI chairman's resignation.

Speaking to reporters on Adiala Road in Rawalpindi, Gohar defended his interaction with Gen Bajwa, saying that there had been no discussion beyond exchanging greetings at the wedding ceremony while condemning what he described as propaganda against him over the encounter.

He said political differences should not be allowed to turn into permanent animosity, adding that relationships could change over time.

“Enemies can become friends and friends can become enemies with the passage of time. Hatred should come to an end,” he said.

Defending his interaction with Gen Bajwa, the PTI chairman said there had been no discussion beyond exchanging greetings at the wedding ceremony while condemning what he described as propaganda against him over the encounter.

Meanwhile, Gohar rejected the possibility of PTI boycotting the upcoming local government elections, saying the party would participate like other political parties.

He said candidates had been directed to prepare their nomination papers for the three constituencies in Islamabad.

The PTI chairman said the PTI did not want confrontation with any state institution, adding that heads of all institutions should remain within their constitutional limits.

Gohar welcomed the Islamabad High Court's order regarding meetings with incarcerated PTI founder Imran Khan, expressing hope that it would be implemented this time.

He said court orders had not been followed for the past two years and that restrictions on meetings with the former prime minister had contributed to political tensions.

The PTI chairman said the information about Imran Khan's health brought by Barrister Salman Safdar after meeting him was not encouraging. He also called for implementation of the Supreme Court's Aug 18 order.

Asked about contacts with the government, Gohar said the party remained in touch with the government and the interior minister, but there were currently no negotiations or backchannel discussions underway.

He said dialogue was necessary to ease political tensions.

Regarding meetings with Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman, Gohar said the discussions had taken place in connection with the proposed All Parties Conference (APC).

He said the two parties could join hands on issues of common concern; however, it was too early to discuss a joint movement.

Commenting on the situation in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa, the PTI chairman said governor's rule or an emergency could not serve as an alternative to a democratic government.

He demanded an end to governor's rule, saying the fact that people had not taken to the streets in protest should not be interpreted as an indication that public anger had subsided.

headline: Rs5tr spent in defiance of law
description: Rs5tr spent in defiance of law
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The federal government has "unconstitutionally" spent over Rs5 trillion on ministries functioning in the provincial domain since the 18th Amendment, according to proceedings of a Senate functional committee panel that on Tuesday barred the release of any further funds for them.

During the meeting, the subcommittee of the Senate's Functional Committee on Devolution also gave a final deadline to the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) to issue orders winding up these ministries, warning that it may have to send a notice to the office if there is no compliance. The office of the auditor general submitted details of spending for the 2011-26 period by ministries functioning in the provincial domain.

More than Rs5 trillion, or $18 billion, has been spent on ministries established in violation of the Constitution since the 18th Amendment, which is more than the $15 billion borrowed from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) during this period, said Senator Zamir Hussain Ghumro, chairman of the committee. He said that had the federal government followed the Constitution and not spent money in areas that are not its responsibility, the country could have avoided the IMF programmes.

The committee instructed the Ministry of Finance, the auditor general and the accountant general to stop releasing funds to ministries working in violation of the Constitution. The proceedings reinforced that Pakistan's problem was not mere taxation but illegal and unconstitutional spending by the federal government, which has been borrowing while continuing to spend in areas that may give it political advantage but add to the debt burden.

According to the details, Rs48.8 billion was unconstitutionally spent over the past 16 years on the Ministry of Climate Change, Rs1.1 trillion on the Ministry of Education, Rs651 billion on the Ministry of Health, Rs398.4 billion on the Ministry of Housing, Rs313 billion on the Ministry of Industries, Rs51.7 billion on the Ministry of Inter-Provincial Coordination, Rs35 billion on the Ministry of Narcotics, Rs270 billion on the Ministry of National Food Security, Rs32 billion on the Ministry of Petroleum, Rs185 billion on the Ministry of Planning, Rs687 billion on the Ministry of Railways and Rs935 billion on the Ministry of Water Resources.

"We are restraining ourselves by not referring the matter of allocating budget to ministries functioning in devolved areas to the National Accountability Bureau under Section 9 for misuse of authority by the Ministry of Finance," Ghumro remarked.

He said the Constitution provided no basis for retaining ministries on the grounds of fulfilling international commitments, adding that under Article 173 provincial governments could also enter into international agreements.

The committee had given the government two weeks to wind up the ministries of health, education, national food security, water resources, climate change, housing, special initiatives, culture and heritage, railways, industries, statistics, petroleum, inter-provincial coordination, narcotics and planning and development.

The committee chairman observed that the panel and the prime minister were aiming at the same thing, saving taxpayers' money and reducing expenditure.

Noreen Bashir, representing the finance ministry, could not give a satisfactory reply and asked Finance Joint Secretary Rashid Zubari to answer the question about the legal authority to release funds to ministries working in devolved areas. He too could not give a satisfactory reply. "You will land in trouble for spending money against the country by allocating budgets to the subjects that have been devolved," Ghumro said, warning the finance ministry representatives.

Cabinet Division Secretary Kamran Afzal also could not report compliance with the committee's instructions to wind up 17 ministries functioning in violation of the Constitution. In light of the committee's instruction a summary had been sent to the Prime Minister's Office, but no instructions had been received, he said.

He acknowledged the committee chairman's knowledge of the Constitution but argued that "there are additional things on the ground". The cabinet secretary was of the view that these ministries are retained because of the practical problems of the "paternalistic role of the federal government and for international coordination".

Ghumro rejected the reply as the "law of necessity", which the committee did not agree to.

For one minister and one federal secretary a ministry is retained in devolved areas, which resulted in over Rs5 trillion of spending in 16 years in violation of the Constitution, he said. The committee noted that under the Constitution international coordination is the responsibility of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, while inter-provincial coordination is the mandate of the Council of Common Interests (CCI). The prime minister heads the CCI while the four chief ministers are its members.

There are also issues, as some provinces are not ready to take responsibility, Afzal said. The cabinet secretary said that for the past two years the federal government has been trying to hand over Sheikh Zayed Hospital, Lahore, and two health institutions in Rawalpindi to the Punjab government, which is refusing to take ownership. The committee chairman said that under the Constitution borrowing is the mandate of the CCI, but the government has not convened a CCI meeting since 2025 and the country was sinking into a debt trap.

The finance ministry is also reluctant to appoint a permanent director general of debt, and the debt office's affairs are run on an ad hoc basis.

headline: Youth loan ceiling raised to Rs25m
description: Youth loan ceiling raised to Rs25m
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Prime Minister's Youth Programme Chairman Rana Mashhood Ahmad Khan has announced that the maximum loan under the Youth Business & Agriculture Loan Scheme has been raised from Rs7.5 million to Rs25 million.

Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, he said the decision, approved by the Economic Coordination Committee and ratified by the federal cabinet, would let successful new businesses grow into real small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs).

A new tier-4 has been introduced that offers loans of over Rs7.5 million and up to Rs25 million at 8% markup for a maximum of eight years. Until now, subsidised loans were capped at Rs7.5 million, leaving successful young businesses with no room to grow.

Tier-4 will support agro-processing, cold chains, mechanised farming, solar energy, manufacturing and exports. "Tier-4 turns today's small business into tomorrow's employer of hundreds," the PMYP chairman remarked.

The scheme is open to youth and adults aged 21 to 45 years and to young people aged 18 and above for IT and e-commerce. New ventures and existing businesses, including farmers, can avail themselves of the scheme and Islamic financing is also available.

The PMYP chairman mentioned that the cost had been reduced for the government while same rates would be applied to borrowers. Banks' margin on tier-3 and tier-4 loans has been cut from Kibor + 3% to Kibor + 2.4%, with no change in the 7-8% rates paid by borrowers. "This saves about Rs0.6 billion on every Rs100 billion disbursed, so more young people can be financed with the same budget," he said.

The government has set a disbursement target of Rs292.5 billion for financial year 2026-27. It plans to extend financing to about 266,700 young Pakistanis, leading to creation of about 835,000 jobs. Funds will be split equally between agriculture and small businesses, and about three in four beneficiaries will receive interest-free tier-1 loans.

Khan revealed that young entrepreneurs had repaid more than 99% of loans, with non-performing loans standing at just 0.74%. "Our young people have repaid more than 99% of what they borrowed. That is not charity; that is credibility," he said. Since the scheme was reconfigured in January 2023, 581,341 young entrepreneurs have been provided financing of Rs313.9 billion, creating an estimated 1.82 million jobs. "This is 10 times the borrowers in the previous decade, achieved in less than four years," he said.

Annual lending has risen from below 17,000 to about 170,000 young people. The scheme has reached 638,081 borrowers by providing Rs392.4 billion and creating nearly 2 million jobs. Since 2023, 62% of the borrowers have been in agriculture and more than 121,000 are young women, one in every five, who have received Rs36.6 billion.

article_html:
ISLAMABAD:

Prime Minister's Youth Programme Chairman Rana Mashhood Ahmad Khan has announced that the maximum loan under the Youth Business & Agriculture Loan Scheme has been raised from Rs7.5 million to Rs25 million.

Addressing a press conference on Tuesday, he said the decision, approved by the Economic Coordination Committee and ratified by the federal cabinet, would let successful new businesses grow into real small and medium-scale enterprises (SMEs).

A new tier-4 has been introduced that offers loans of over Rs7.5 million and up to Rs25 million at 8% markup for a maximum of eight years. Until now, subsidised loans were capped at Rs7.5 million, leaving successful young businesses with no room to grow.

Tier-4 will support agro-processing, cold chains, mechanised farming, solar energy, manufacturing and exports. "Tier-4 turns today's small business into tomorrow's employer of hundreds," the PMYP chairman remarked.

The scheme is open to youth and adults aged 21 to 45 years and to young people aged 18 and above for IT and e-commerce. New ventures and existing businesses, including farmers, can avail themselves of the scheme and Islamic financing is also available.

The PMYP chairman mentioned that the cost had been reduced for the government while same rates would be applied to borrowers. Banks' margin on tier-3 and tier-4 loans has been cut from Kibor + 3% to Kibor + 2.4%, with no change in the 7-8% rates paid by borrowers. "This saves about Rs0.6 billion on every Rs100 billion disbursed, so more young people can be financed with the same budget," he said.

The government has set a disbursement target of Rs292.5 billion for financial year 2026-27. It plans to extend financing to about 266,700 young Pakistanis, leading to creation of about 835,000 jobs. Funds will be split equally between agriculture and small businesses, and about three in four beneficiaries will receive interest-free tier-1 loans.

Khan revealed that young entrepreneurs had repaid more than 99% of loans, with non-performing loans standing at just 0.74%. "Our young people have repaid more than 99% of what they borrowed. That is not charity; that is credibility," he said. Since the scheme was reconfigured in January 2023, 581,341 young entrepreneurs have been provided financing of Rs313.9 billion, creating an estimated 1.82 million jobs. "This is 10 times the borrowers in the previous decade, achieved in less than four years," he said.

Annual lending has risen from below 17,000 to about 170,000 young people. The scheme has reached 638,081 borrowers by providing Rs392.4 billion and creating nearly 2 million jobs. Since 2023, 62% of the borrowers have been in agriculture and more than 121,000 are young women, one in every five, who have received Rs36.6 billion.

headline: SME financing doubles to Rs1.2tr in 2 years
description: SME financing doubles to Rs1.2tr in 2 years
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Pakistan's banking sector has more than doubled financing to small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to Rs1.2 trillion over the past two years, from around Rs490 billion, while the number of borrowers has increased from 200,000 to 350,000, Pakistan Banks Association (PBA) Chairman Zafar Masud said on Tuesday.

Speaking during a visit to the Karachi Press Club alongside PBA Chief Executive Muneer Kamal, Masud said the banking industry had made significant progress in expanding credit to smaller businesses, farmers and households as part of efforts to promote financial inclusion and economic growth. He said the number of agricultural borrowers had also recovered to 3.4 million from 2.7 million, after declining from 4 million in 2019. The State Bank of Pakistan has set a target of increasing agricultural borrowers to 5.8 million by 2028. Agricultural financing is expected to rise from Rs1.3 trillion to Rs3.3 trillion during this period.

In housing finance, the number of borrowers has increased from 65,000 two years ago to around 300,000, while approved financing has reached Rs455 billion, Masud said. He cited government-backed housing finance programmes as contributing to the expansion. Masud said banks had also restructured Rs1.3 trillion in loans to the energy sector without government guarantees, helping address circular debt. He added that a charge of Rs3.23 per unit on electricity bills was expected to be phased out over the next two years. The banking sector also played a role in facilitating the privatisation of Pakistan International Airlines (PIA) by restructuring around Rs300 billion in debt, he said.

On export promotion, Masud said banks continued to provide financing to exporters at 4%, despite higher policy rates. The banking industry was bearing an estimated Rs100 billion in costs to maintain concessional financing for exporters.

He said banks were also taking over the financial burden of facilitating remittances from overseas Pakistanis after the government discontinued its incentive payments from July 1, 2026. The banking industry would spend approximately Rs100 billion annually to ensure remittances could be sent to Pakistan without transfer charges.

headline: Remittances nearly cover trade gap
description: Remittances nearly cover trade gap
author: Usman Hanif
article_text:
Pakistan's workers' remittances rose to a four-month high of $3.9 billion in October, taking cumulative inflows during the first four months of FY27 to $14.77 billion, almost enough to cover the country's entire merchandise trade deficit of $14.6 billion during the same period.

The latest figures highlight the growing importance of overseas Pakistanis in supporting the external account, as inflows continued to cushion the widening trade gap and helped contain pressure on foreign exchange reserves.

According to data released by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) on Tuesday, October remittances increased 13.8% year-on-year from $3.42 billion and rose 8.5% month-on-month from $3.59 billion in September, the highest monthly inflow recorded so far in FY27. During July to October, remittances increased 14% to $14.77 billion, against $12.96 billion in the corresponding period last year.

JS Global Head of Equity Research and Senior Vice President Waqas Ghani said, "Overseas Pakistanis just covered almost the entire trade deficit, again." He pointed out that remittances of $14.8 billion during the first four months compared with a merchandise trade deficit of $14.6 billion, which had widened 16% year-on-year.

Sustained inflows, particularly from Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies, are helping contain pressure on the current account, support foreign exchange reserves and strengthen the country's external financing position, he said. He added that channel checks indicated economic activity in the Gulf was also recovering, reinforcing the resilience of remittance flows from GCC economies and providing continued support to the external account. "Remittances are buying Pakistan time. The question is whether exports can catch up or nah," he remarked.

Gulf economies remain the biggest source

Country-wise data showed Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates remained the largest sources, contributing $3.67 billion and $3.05 billion respectively during July to October.

Together, the two accounted for around 45.5% of total inflows. Including other GCC countries, the region contributed approximately $8.09 billion, or 54.8% of the total.

Saudi Arabia's remittances increased 16.5% year-on-year, while inflows from the UAE grew 13.5%. Among other GCC economies, Bahrain recorded growth of 15.8%, Kuwait 13.9% and Qatar 13.6%. Within the UAE, Dubai remained the dominant contributor, with remittances rising 28% to $2.51 billion. Inflows from Abu Dhabi, by contrast, declined 29.5% to $443.2 million, indicating diverging trends within the country's major corridors.

UK outpaces US as European inflows grow

Outside the Gulf, the United Kingdom emerged as the largest source, sending $2.23 billion during the first four months, up 19.2% from a year earlier.

Inflows from the United States increased 13.8% to $1.26 billion, while remittances from European Union countries rose 9.6% to $1.87 billion.

Italy contributed $565.2 million, Spain $339.9 million and Germany $282.5 million during the period.

Australia and Canada also maintained positive growth, with remittances rising 12.9% to $386.9 million and 11.5% to $268.9 million respectively. The figures indicate that while the Gulf remains the backbone of remittance inflows, overseas Pakistanis in the UK, Europe, North America and Australia continue to provide an important source of foreign exchange.

Sustained growth offers some relief to the external financing position, though the widening trade deficit underscores the need to strengthen export earnings and reduce reliance on overseas transfers to finance external payments. The rupee continued its marginal appreciation against the US dollar in the interbank market on Tuesday, closing at Rs276.65, up Rs0.01 from the previous session. It had gained 0.03%, or Re0.09, last week to settle at Rs276.66, against Rs276.75 a week earlier, according to SBP data.

Gold prices declined on Tuesday, tracking losses in the international market, with 24-karat gold falling Rs1,500 per tola to Rs430,836.

The price of 10-gram gold dropped Rs1,286 to Rs369,372, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association (APGJSA). In the previous session, gold had increased Rs3,200 per tola to Rs432,336.

In the international market, gold fell $15 to $4,083 per ounce, while silver remained unchanged at Rs5,723 per tola in the local market.

article_html:
KARACHI:

Pakistan's workers' remittances rose to a four-month high of $3.9 billion in October, taking cumulative inflows during the first four months of FY27 to $14.77 billion, almost enough to cover the country's entire merchandise trade deficit of $14.6 billion during the same period.

The latest figures highlight the growing importance of overseas Pakistanis in supporting the external account, as inflows continued to cushion the widening trade gap and helped contain pressure on foreign exchange reserves.

According to data released by the State Bank of Pakistan (SBP) on Tuesday, October remittances increased 13.8% year-on-year from $3.42 billion and rose 8.5% month-on-month from $3.59 billion in September, the highest monthly inflow recorded so far in FY27. During July to October, remittances increased 14% to $14.77 billion, against $12.96 billion in the corresponding period last year.

JS Global Head of Equity Research and Senior Vice President Waqas Ghani said, "Overseas Pakistanis just covered almost the entire trade deficit, again." He pointed out that remittances of $14.8 billion during the first four months compared with a merchandise trade deficit of $14.6 billion, which had widened 16% year-on-year.

Sustained inflows, particularly from Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) economies, are helping contain pressure on the current account, support foreign exchange reserves and strengthen the country's external financing position, he said. He added that channel checks indicated economic activity in the Gulf was also recovering, reinforcing the resilience of remittance flows from GCC economies and providing continued support to the external account. "Remittances are buying Pakistan time. The question is whether exports can catch up or nah," he remarked.

Gulf economies remain the biggest source

Country-wise data showed Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates remained the largest sources, contributing $3.67 billion and $3.05 billion respectively during July to October.

Together, the two accounted for around 45.5% of total inflows. Including other GCC countries, the region contributed approximately $8.09 billion, or 54.8% of the total.

Saudi Arabia's remittances increased 16.5% year-on-year, while inflows from the UAE grew 13.5%. Among other GCC economies, Bahrain recorded growth of 15.8%, Kuwait 13.9% and Qatar 13.6%. Within the UAE, Dubai remained the dominant contributor, with remittances rising 28% to $2.51 billion. Inflows from Abu Dhabi, by contrast, declined 29.5% to $443.2 million, indicating diverging trends within the country's major corridors.

UK outpaces US as European inflows grow

Outside the Gulf, the United Kingdom emerged as the largest source, sending $2.23 billion during the first four months, up 19.2% from a year earlier.

Inflows from the United States increased 13.8% to $1.26 billion, while remittances from European Union countries rose 9.6% to $1.87 billion.

Italy contributed $565.2 million, Spain $339.9 million and Germany $282.5 million during the period.

Australia and Canada also maintained positive growth, with remittances rising 12.9% to $386.9 million and 11.5% to $268.9 million respectively. The figures indicate that while the Gulf remains the backbone of remittance inflows, overseas Pakistanis in the UK, Europe, North America and Australia continue to provide an important source of foreign exchange.

Sustained growth offers some relief to the external financing position, though the widening trade deficit underscores the need to strengthen export earnings and reduce reliance on overseas transfers to finance external payments. The rupee continued its marginal appreciation against the US dollar in the interbank market on Tuesday, closing at Rs276.65, up Rs0.01 from the previous session. It had gained 0.03%, or Re0.09, last week to settle at Rs276.66, against Rs276.75 a week earlier, according to SBP data.

Gold prices declined on Tuesday, tracking losses in the international market, with 24-karat gold falling Rs1,500 per tola to Rs430,836.

The price of 10-gram gold dropped Rs1,286 to Rs369,372, according to rates released by the All-Pakistan Gems and Jewellers Sarafa Association (APGJSA). In the previous session, gold had increased Rs3,200 per tola to Rs432,336.

In the international market, gold fell $15 to $4,083 per ounce, while silver remained unchanged at Rs5,723 per tola in the local market.

headline: Oil prices slide 2% to two-month low
description: Oil prices slide 2% to two-month low
author: Reuters
article_text:
Brent futures fell $1.93, or 2.1%, to $90.64 a barrel

Oil prices slid about 2% to fresh two-month lows on Tuesday after US officials downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran, easing fears of further Middle East supply disruptions.

Brent futures fell $1.93, or 2.1%, to $90.64 a barrel at 1528 GMT, while US WTI crude fell $1.44, or 1.7%, to $85.41. That put both crude benchmarks on track for their lowest close since August 28. On Monday, both contracts closed at their lowest since August 31.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday that he told Group of Seven allies that the US economic sanctions and naval blockade were working so well that President Donald Trump did not need to conduct major combat operations in Iran. Rubio made the comments during a meeting in Paris of foreign ministers from the G7.

On Monday, Trump said he plans to hold off on new military strikes against Iran for the time being after appeals from countries in the region, including from Qatar's prime minister in White House talks.

headline: 9pm closure cuts retail sales by 42%
description: 9pm closure cuts retail sales by 42%
author: SHAHRAM HAQ
article_text:
The early closing rule for shops in Pakistan has cut daily transactions at retail outlets by 42%, while evidence that it has saved energy remains thin, according to a new study by research firm Ipsos presented by the Chainstore Association of Pakistan.

Retailers in provinces where the 9pm closing time applies said their shops now open 1.6 hours less each day, with average operating hours falling from 11.2 to 9.6. Across the top 10 product categories, the average number of transactions per shop fell from 86 to 50 a day. Footwear saw one of the sharpest drops, from 85 to 38.

The survey further found that the share of retailers rating their overall sales as good fell from 79% before the rule to 34% now, while those reporting high profitability dropped from 67% to 26%. The share seeing heavy evening footfall between 4pm and 8pm halved from 63% to 32%. A head of e-commerce at a footwear and apparel brand said 40% to 50% of a day's footfall comes between 7pm and 9pm.

The rule was meant to save energy, but the survey found little proof. While 56% of retailers said the goal was achieved, only 41% saw their own utility bills fall. In Punjab, Islamabad and Balochistan, where the 9pm rule is still in force, the figure was just 31%. Even retailers who believe the rule saved energy reported daily transactions falling from 108 to 50.

Half of the 300 retailers interviewed oppose the rule and 32% support it. Opposition rises to 54% among owners, who set trading hours. Among retailers who believed energy goals were met, only one in five wanted the rule to continue unchanged. Another 57% wanted the timings changed and 21% wanted the rule removed.

Shops have adjusted. About 73% now open earlier in the day, 34% have started or expanded online sales and 12% have cut staff. A footwear executive warned against assuming customers have moved online.

Consumers are divided. Of 1,046 people surveyed, 35% support early closing, 33% are neutral and 32% oppose it. But 37% said their shopping experience worsened, against 23% who said it improved. Some 53% said finding time to shop has become harder, while only 15% found it easier.

Shopping habits have shifted. Those preferring to shop after 8pm fell from 9% to 4%. Average monthly trips dropped from 9.4 to 8.7, but women cut back far more, from 7.2 to 5.8 trips, a fall of 19%, against 3% for men. Neighbourhood shops gained ground, rising from 27% to 31% as the most used format, while malls slipped from 8% to 6%. People who rarely or never shop for leisure rose from 74% to 87%.

The study also compared 15 countries. Only Bangladesh, which has changed its closing time seven times since April, shuts shops early to save energy. Malls in most benchmark countries stay open until 10pm or later. Brazil, the Philippines, Indonesia, France and Dubai have cut power use through quotas, peak-hour tariffs and efficiency plans without ordering shops to close.

Stakeholders also criticised how the policy was made. Ten of the 25 key informants said traders were not consulted. "Until you take traders into confidence and develop policies in consultation with them, the situation will not improve," said the president of a market traders' association. A senior executive at a national apparel chain said adjusting to new timings takes four to six weeks, and "by the time we adjust, they change it again".

Ten informants said enforcement was uneven or heavy-handed. Seven suggested later closing at 10pm to 11pm. Five proposed targeting energy directly, through solar power, electric vehicles and reducing power leakage.

Sindh and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa lifted the rule on May 16, 2026. The fieldwork was conducted between August and September 2026 across 53 malls and markets in 10 cities, the survey added.

article_html:
LAHORE:

The early closing rule for shops in Pakistan has cut daily transactions at retail outlets by 42%, while evidence that it has saved energy remains thin, according to a new study by research firm Ipsos presented by the Chainstore Association of Pakistan.

Retailers in provinces where the 9pm closing time applies said their shops now open 1.6 hours less each day, with average operating hours falling from 11.2 to 9.6. Across the top 10 product categories, the average number of transactions per shop fell from 86 to 50 a day. Footwear saw one of the sharpest drops, from 85 to 38.

The survey further found that the share of retailers rating their overall sales as good fell from 79% before the rule to 34% now, while those reporting high profitability dropped from 67% to 26%. The share seeing heavy evening footfall between 4pm and 8pm halved from 63% to 32%. A head of e-commerce at a footwear and apparel brand said 40% to 50% of a day's footfall comes between 7pm and 9pm.

The rule was meant to save energy, but the survey found little proof. While 56% of retailers said the goal was achieved, only 41% saw their own utility bills fall. In Punjab, Islamabad and Balochistan, where the 9pm rule is still in force, the figure was just 31%. Even retailers who believe the rule saved energy reported daily transactions falling from 108 to 50.

Half of the 300 retailers interviewed oppose the rule and 32% support it. Opposition rises to 54% among owners, who set trading hours. Among retailers who believed energy goals were met, only one in five wanted the rule to continue unchanged. Another 57% wanted the timings changed and 21% wanted the rule removed.

Shops have adjusted. About 73% now open earlier in the day, 34% have started or expanded online sales and 12% have cut staff. A footwear executive warned against assuming customers have moved online.

Consumers are divided. Of 1,046 people surveyed, 35% support early closing, 33% are neutral and 32% oppose it. But 37% said their shopping experience worsened, against 23% who said it improved. Some 53% said finding time to shop has become harder, while only 15% found it easier.

Shopping habits have shifted. Those preferring to shop after 8pm fell from 9% to 4%. Average monthly trips dropped from 9.4 to 8.7, but women cut back far more, from 7.2 to 5.8 trips, a fall of 19%, against 3% for men. Neighbourhood shops gained ground, rising from 27% to 31% as the most used format, while malls slipped from 8% to 6%. People who rarely or never shop for leisure rose from 74% to 87%.

The study also compared 15 countries. Only Bangladesh, which has changed its closing time seven times since April, shuts shops early to save energy. Malls in most benchmark countries stay open until 10pm or later. Brazil, the Philippines, Indonesia, France and Dubai have cut power use through quotas, peak-hour tariffs and efficiency plans without ordering shops to close.

Stakeholders also criticised how the policy was made. Ten of the 25 key informants said traders were not consulted. "Until you take traders into confidence and develop policies in consultation with them, the situation will not improve," said the president of a market traders' association. A senior executive at a national apparel chain said adjusting to new timings takes four to six weeks, and "by the time we adjust, they change it again".

Ten informants said enforcement was uneven or heavy-handed. Seven suggested later closing at 10pm to 11pm. Five proposed targeting energy directly, through solar power, electric vehicles and reducing power leakage.

Sindh and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa lifted the rule on May 16, 2026. The fieldwork was conducted between August and September 2026 across 53 malls and markets in 10 cities, the survey added.

headline: Import-centric auto policy under fire
description: Import-centric auto policy under fire
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Pakistan's newly announced auto policy has drawn strong criticism from the domestic automotive parts industry, which warns that its import-centric approach could undermine local manufacturing, threaten 300,000 direct jobs and increase pressure on foreign exchange reserves.

Former President of the Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers (PAAPAM) Aamir Allawala said the policy favoured imports of completely built-up electric vehicles and completely knocked-down kits over domestic manufacturing, putting nearly 1,200 engineering and component manufacturing enterprises at risk.

He said the policy could reverse years of progress in localisation, currently estimated at 50% to 65% for several locally assembled models, and that assemblers would find it more economical to import components from foreign partners rather than procure them locally, threatening 300,000 direct jobs and another 1.5 million indirectly associated with the industry.

Increased vehicle imports would create additional demand for foreign exchange, while tax concessions on imported electric vehicles could widen the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR)'s revenue gap, he warned.

Allawala argued that consumers, representing only around 0.1% of the population who buy cars annually, might benefit from a 5% to 7% price reduction, but questioned whether these limited gains justified damage to the wider industrial ecosystem. He said component manufacturers had not endorsed the policy, claiming its final version was substantially different from proposals discussed with the Ministry of Industries and Production up to June 2026.

He suggested renaming it from the "Auto and Auto Parts Policy" to the "Policy for Automobile Assembly and Import of New and Used Vehicles", arguing its incentives primarily benefited imports rather than local manufacturing.

Former PAAPAM chairman Abdul Rehman Aizaz described the policy as import-centred and warned that cutting customs duty on completely built-up vehicles to 15% by 2031 would undermine the entire domestic value chain, with consequences extending beyond component makers to material producers including Aisha Steel, International Steels and People's Steel Mills, as well as local assemblers.

He questioned how Pakistan could compete when India, Thailand and Indonesia impose completely built-up import duties of around 120%, 80% and 52% respectively, against the proposed 15%, warning that around 300,000 direct jobs could disappear by 2031 if domestic production became commercially unviable.

Aizaz also raised concerns over concessions for new energy vehicles, particularly the proposed 15% localisation target over five years, saying low import duties on electric vehicles and components could shift manufacturing and employment abroad. He questioned facilitating commercial imports of used vehicles without an age limit, saying it contradicted the stated objective of reducing carbon emissions.

Auto expert Mashood Ali Khan said two successive policies covering 2016-21 and 2021-26 had failed to deliver meaningful localisation, with companies offered a 25% incentive to establish local manufacturing but many continuing to import components. He questioned how localisation would be achieved when the completely built-up tariff would fall to 15% by 2031, noting Pakistan had already reached around 65% localisation in several categories.

He urged binding localisation requirements for every new model, with at least 10% of components made locally at launch and an annual roadmap for increasing domestic content and questioned the $6 billion export target envisaging equal contributions from parts makers and original equipment manufacturers.

The Pakistan Automotive Manufacturers Association called the policy a need of the time and asked the ministry for an official copy of the policy for its members.

Auto expert Mashood Ali Khan said two successive policies covering 2016-21 and 2021-26 had failed to deliver meaningful localisation, with companies offered a 25% incentive to establish local manufacturing but many continuing to import components. He questioned how localisation would be achieved when the completely built-up tariff would fall to 15% by 2031, noting Pakistan had already reached around 65% localisation in several categories.

He urged binding localisation requirements for every new model, with at least 10% of components made locally at launch and an annual roadmap for increasing domestic content and questioned the $6 billion export target envisaging equal contributions from parts makers and original equipment manufacturers.
The Pakistan Automotive Manufacturers Association called the policy a need of the time and asked the ministry for an official copy of the policy for its members.

headline: Pakistan backs global green freight push
description: Pakistan backs global green freight push
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Federal Minister for Communications Abdul Aleem Khan endorsed the Global Green Freight Corridors Initiative at a high-level ministerial roundtable during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, and pledged Pakistan's support for pilot green corridors, according to an official statement issued on Tuesday.

The roundtable was co-hosted by Turkish Minister for Transport and Infrastructure Abdulkadir Uraloglu, the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE) and the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific and brought together global leaders to address sustainable transit solutions.

He said international freight transport was the lifeblood of global commerce but one of the fastest-growing sources of transport-related greenhouse gas emissions, and that economic growth and environmental stewardship were mutually reinforcing goals.

He said the initiative showed sustainable logistics was the only viable path forward and that COP31 must shift focus toward turning international climate pledges into tangible cross-border outcomes. The minister reaffirmed Pakistan's commitment to decarbonising global supply chains and building climate-resilient logistics infrastructure.

Pakistan is strategically placed as a regional trade bridge linking China, Central Asia and the Middle East, with a network of over 500,000 kilometres of roads, a 7,800-kilometre railway, major deep-sea ports and developing trade arteries under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, he said. Road carries 96% of domestic freight, straining national resources and urban air quality, and Pakistan is pursuing a multi-pillar transition, he said.

The Railway Plan 2026 aims to lift rail's freight share to 20% through the modernised Main Line-1 (ML-1) project, alongside the National Electric Vehicle Policy 2025-30, which provides for 3,000 charging stations along major corridors, and complementary maritime reforms across national seaports.

He said TIR transit volumes had risen 200% under the UN TIR Convention, with digital pre-shipment notices integrated into the Pakistan Single Window and an eTIR project with UNECE, positioning Pakistan as one of the fastest-rising countries in regional trade facilitation.

Financing combines Public Sector Development Programme allocations, multilateral support from the Asian Development Bank and Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, and private investment under the Public-Private Partnership Authority Act for projects including the M-6 Motorway and ML-1 upgrades, he said.

headline: PSX jumps 5,449 points in spectacular rally
description: PSX jumps 5,449 points in spectacular rally
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) staged a powerful rally on Tuesday as investors returned from the long weekend with renewed buying interest, driving the KSE-100 index up by over 5,400 points amid support from strong remittances and easing international oil prices.

The benchmark index settled at 179,335.24, surging 5,448.56 points, or 3.13%. It remained in positive territory throughout the session and touched the intra-day high of 179,424.04, while the day's low was 176,273.72. The market reopened following a public holiday on Monday on account of Iqbal Day. The return of investors coincided with improving domestic and international developments, triggering across-the-board buying.

On the domestic front, strong remittance inflows helped reinforce investor confidence by supporting the country's external account. Meanwhile, the decline in international oil prices provided additional relief following concerns over Pakistan's exposure to imported energy and the potential impact of higher fuel costs on inflation and the balance of payments. Crude prices extended losses on Tuesday after President Trump downplayed the need for further military action, easing fears of continued supply disruptions in the Middle East.

According to Arif Habib Limited Deputy Head of Trading Ali Najib, the PSX extended its bullish momentum for another session, firmly reclaiming the 175k psychological mark. The market opened on a positive note, buoyed by a sharp correction in global oil prices following the Democrats' sweeping gains in the US midterm elections. WTI crude dipped below $87/barrel, while Brent fell to $96/barrel from the previous session's $102/barrel, marking a decline of over 8%, he said.

The sharp retreat in oil prices improved investor sentiment, which triggered broad-based buying and helped the benchmark index reclaim the 175k level for the first time since September 1, 2026. In the US, the Democrats' gains in elections fuelled optimism about a potential de-escalation in the Middle East and supported a broader recovery in the global risk appetite, Najib said.

UBL, Lucky Cement, Meezan Bank, Systems Ltd, Engro Holdings, Bank AL Habib, HBL, Hub Power, Oil & Gas Development Company and Pakistan Petroleum were the major contributors to the rally, collectively adding 1,981 points to the index. "Going forward, the market is likely to maintain its bullish momentum amid easing oil prices and improved global risk appetite. However, profit-taking may emerge at higher levels, keeping investors selective and cautious," he added.

Topline Securities observed that investor sentiment remained upbeat amid easing international oil prices and diminishing concerns over a potential escalation in geopolitical tensions between the US and Iran. UBL, FFC, HUBC, LUCK and MEBL emerged as the leading positive contributors, collectively adding 1,982 points to the index and providing significant support to the market's overall performance, it said.

Cumulatively, trading volumes decreased to 972.4 million shares from Friday's tally of 1.5 billion. The value of traded shares stood at Rs50.7 billion.

Shares of 501 companies were traded in the ready market. Of these, 363 stocks closed higher, 107 fell and 31 remained unchanged.

Cnergyico Pk was the volume leader with trading in 70.1 million shares, falling Rs0.75 to close at Rs11.35. Foreign investors bought shares worth Rs1.68 billion, the National Clearing Company reported.

headline: Pakistan to produce FMD vaccines in a year
description: Pakistan to produce FMD vaccines in a year
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
Pakistan and Turkiye have agreed to further strengthen bilateral cooperation in the livestock sector, particularly in the areas of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) control, vaccine manufacturing, livestock development and meat exports.

The understanding was reached during a meeting between Federal Minister for National Food Security and Research Rana Tanveer Hussain and Turkiye Minister of Agriculture and Forestry Ibrahim Yumakli.

Hussain told his Turkish counterpart that Pakistan was pursuing the establishment of facilities for manufacturing FMD vaccines within one year. In this regard, two projects are being undertaken – one by the government of Punjab and the other at the federal level. He stated that Pakistan intended to export meat to Turkiye following the successful completion of the FMD-free zone. Both sides agreed to pursue cooperation in these areas for mutual benefit.

The food minister emphasised that Pakistan was keen to benefit from Turkiye's experience in livestock development, disease control and vaccine production. He voiced confidence that enhanced bilateral cooperation would contribute to strengthening Pakistan's livestock sector and opening new avenues for agricultural trade.

headline: Faysal Quraishi responds to 'Mango Jutt' criticism
description: Faysal Quraishi responds to 'Mango Jutt' criticism
author: Qaisar Kamran
article_text:
Film festivals are not just about watching movies; they also provide filmmakers, artists and enthusiasts an opportunity to connect, exchange ideas and learn about the process of filmmaking.

Speaking on the sidelines of the World Culture Festival, Pakistani filmmaker said that film enthusiasts look forward to such festivals every year, as they offer more than just screenings. Filmmakers from different countries also attend to represent their work, making the event an opportunity for meaningful interaction and discussion.

He said that such gatherings allow filmmakers to understand how projects are initiated and how the filmmaking process begins. The initial discussions and exchange of ideas are particularly important for those working in the industry.

"These festivals also inspire young people. If they want to pursue filmmaking, they get to see different pathways and understand how they can move forward and create better work," he said.

Asked about the audience response after his film was screened at the cinema and later at the World Culture Festival, as well as the criticism it received on social media following its release, the filmmaker said that many viewers had enjoyed the film.

"Not every film is going to be liked by everyone. Even after watching a film like The Odyssey, some people come out saying, 'What did I just watch? What kind of film was that?' So, our film can also have shortcomings. There is nothing unusual about someone not liking it," he said.

Faysal Quraishi is one of Pakistan's highest-paid actors. He is the recipient of more than 20 nationally recognised awards. He first gained recognition for playing the leading role of Boota in the television series Boota from Toba Tek Singh (1999) and has been a part of more than 200 projects. Quraishi hosted a morning show called Muskurati Morning with Faisal Qureshi from 2010 to 2014. From 2016 to 2019, he hosted the morning show Salam Zindagi. He made his film acting debut in 1992. He became a producer in 2017 with the production house Connect Studios, and owns a film production house named Faysal Quraishi Films.

He added that social media had given everyone a platform to express their opinions, and he was open to both appreciation and criticism.

"Some people praised the film, while others did not like it. That's fine. It is good that people are sharing their feedback," he said.

Clarifying his response to the criticism circulating online, he said that the video he had shared was not directed at any particular individual. Rather, it was a response to a message that had reached him.

headline: Sister seeks health transfer for Imran
description: Sister seeks health transfer for Imran
author: Hasnaat Malik
article_text:
As neither the Supreme Court nor the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) has fixed a date for hearing the matter concerning former prime minister Imran Khan's transfer from Adiala Jail to a private medical facility, an application has been filed in the SC on behalf of his sister, Uzma Khan, seeking early hearing of the case.

Uzma Khan, who has herself been detained under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO) at Kot Lakhpat Jail for the past couple of months, has moved an application requesting the apex court to urgently take up the matter concerning Imran Khan's transfer from Adiala Jail to Shifa International Hospital in compliance with its August 18 order.

Earlier, Senator Mashal Yousafzai had also filed an application seeking early hearing of the case.

Uzma Khan had already filed a contempt petition against the prime minister and other executive authorities over their alleged failure to implement the August 18 order.

The latest application has also urged the court to depute one of its officers or appoint a local commission to oversee Imran Khan's transfer to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination.

Explaining the urgency, the applicant submitted that, according to reports circulating in the media, Imran Khan's blood pressure had recently risen to 192, raising serious concerns about his health.

"If an early hearing of this matter is not granted, the applicant's and Imran Khan guaranteed rights will continue to be prejudiced in particular, his fundamental right to health and well-being, access to medical advice and facilities as well as to members of his family will continue to be violated."

The application further stated: "The material showing the precarious state of his health and the widespread public concern about it has already been filed with the petition."

The SC has also been requested to fix the main case for hearing next week.

Meanwhile, on September 14, the FCC summoned the record of the case concerning Imran Khan's health from the SC.

Subsequently, on September 16, a three-member bench headed by Justice Shahid Waheed raised questions about the FCC's order. During the hearing, Attorney General for Pakistan Mansoor Awan sought three weeks to assist the SC in the matter.

Despite the passage of two months, the SC has not fixed the matter for hearing. The FCC, meanwhile, listed the three-prisoners case in which it had sought the record of Imran Khan's health-related case.

A lawyer believes that the matter's continued absence from the cause lists of both courts suggests there may be an informal understanding between the SC and the FCC.

He said that instead of allowing the matter to linger, the jurisdictional question between the two apex courts needed to be resolved.

headline: PM arrives in Turkiye for COP31 summit

author: Our Correspondent
article_text:

headline: Govt seeks smart meters to curb power theft, overbilling
description: Govt seeks smart meters to curb power theft, overbilling
author: Our Correspondent
article_text:
The government is working to secure funding for installing smart meters on transformers across all power distribution companies (DISCOs) with plans to ensure the project continues even after their privatisation.

The initiative is aimed at curbing electricity theft, improving billing accuracy and protecting consumers from overbilling, according to a statement issued after a meeting chaired by Minister for Economic Affairs and Establishment Division Ahad Cheema on Tuesday.

The meeting reviewed development programmes for DISCOs and the Economic Affairs Division's efforts to arrange financing for the smart metering system. Participants were informed that progress had been made in securing funding for the project.

The meeting also discussed arrangements for continuing the initiative after privatisation. Cheema said the government would ensure that private investors took the project forward following the transfer of the distribution companies.

He said negotiations with multilateral development partners for financing development programmes would continue until the privatisation process was completed. In cases where a DISCO was privatised while negotiations or programme preparations were still under way, the relevant financing and development programmes would be transferred to the private investor as part of the handover, subject to agreed arrangements.

Cheema further said any new project undertaken by a private investor within a DISCO would have to go through competitive bidding and obtain approval from the National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (Nepra), where applicable.

He stressed that privatisation should not result in additional costs or undue financial pressure on consumers, adding that the government would facilitate the process while protecting consumer interests and ensuring investors fulfilled their financial and contractual obligations.

headline: Ex-MPA Achakzai gets 10 years in prison
description: Ex-MPA Achakzai gets 10 years in prison
author: Sardar Hameed Khan
article_text:
The Balochistan High Court (BHC) on Tuesday accepted the provincial government's appeal against the acquittal of Pashtunkhwa Milli Awami Party (PMAP) leader, former provincial lawmaker and Public Accounts Committee chairman Abdul Majeed Achakzai, sentencing him to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment in a case involving the death of traffic sub-inspector Haji Ataullah.

The court also ordered him to pay blood money to the legal heirs of the deceased.

According to the BHC, a division bench comprising Justice Muhammad Aamir Nawaz Rana and Justice Abdul Qayyum Lehri heard the government's appeal against Achakzai's acquittal.

The court accepted the appeal and set aside the acquittal verdict announced on September 4, 2020, by the Additional Sessions Judge-VI and Model Criminal Trial Court-II, Quetta.

The high court convicted Achakzai under Section 320 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC) for causing the death of traffic sub-inspector Haji Ataullah, who was on duty, by running him over while driving recklessly and negligently at high speed.

The court sentenced Achakzai to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment and ordered him to pay blood money to the deceased's legal heirs.

The high court directed the Additional Sessions Judge-VI, Quetta, to issue non-bailable arrest warrants for Achakzai, who is currently out on bail, for his immediate arrest and the implementation of the sentence.

The court also directed the relevant authorities to ensure prompt execution of the arrest warrants in accordance with the law so that Achakzai could be transferred to prison to serve his sentence.

The case

The incident took place on June 20, 2017, at GPO Chowk on Zarghoon Road in Quetta, where a speeding official Land Cruiser belonging to Achakzai hit traffic sergeant Haji Ataullah Dashti, who was on duty. Dashti sustained serious injuries and later died, while a cyclist, Abdul Ghafoor Baloch, was also injured.

Achakzai allegedly ran over the traffic sergeant after the latter signalled him to stop. The incident, initially treated as a traffic accident, came under scrutiny after CCTV footage emerged showing the vehicle hitting the officer following an exchange of words between the two.

The footage went viral on social media and prompted protests by the Balochistan press. There were also reports that Achakzai was driving recklessly and was intoxicated at the time.

Police initially registered a case against unidentified persons. Following the emergence of the footage, they registered a case against Achakzai on charges of terrorism, murder, and attempted murder. He was arrested from his residence in Quetta's Satellite Town area on June 25, 2017.

Civil Lines police subsequently submitted a challan before the Anti-Terrorism Court, but the terrorism charge was later withdrawn after police failed to establish it.

Achakzai, who was elected to the Balochistan Assembly from PB-13 Qila Abdullah in the 2013 general elections, admitted that he had been driving his official vehicle when the incident occurred. He said he would compensate the deceased traffic sergeant's family and the injured passerby. He also intended to travel to Dera Ghazi Khan with tribal elders to meet Dashti's family.

The case was later transferred to the Model Criminal Trial Court in Quetta, where it remained under trial for around three years.

On September 4, 2020, the Model Criminal Trial Court acquitted Achakzai, ruling that the prosecution had failed to establish that he was driving the vehicle when the incident occurred.

In its 29-page written judgment, Judge Dost Muhammad Mandokhail noted that none of the 20 prosecution witnesses, including eyewitnesses and the deceased's brother, had identified Achakzai as the driver of the vehicle.
